# 03. Death, difficulty and progression

Every roguelike makes a promise about losing. The character will die, the run will end, and the player will start again, many times. This chapter is about keeping that promise worth accepting: why permadeath is there at all, what makes a death feel earned, how long the walk back to the interesting part should be, how much of a run should survive its end, and how randomness, clocks, pacing, power, balance and difficulty settings shape the run that death interrupts. For a designer these are not separate topics. A loss that feels arbitrary, a restart that takes too long, a grind that quietly wins more games than skill does: each one turns a game built to be replayed into a game players stop replaying.

The talks come at the subject from many directions: Rogue's authors explaining why its actions cannot be undone ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 28:32](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1712)), developers of long-lived traditional roguelikes looking back at how their players actually played ([Nick McConnell 2021, 7:13](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=433); [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 19:59](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1199)), designers of roguelites and deckbuilders arguing for meta-progression and difficulty options, board-game and card-game designers bringing push-your-luck and variance from the table, and players who set themselves harder rules than any designer did. They agree more than you might expect about what a good death looks like and about the danger of tedious optimal play. They disagree, usefully, about how much to soften death, how much power to carry between runs, and how much randomness to smooth away.

## In brief

- Permadeath is better understood as consequence persistence: irreversibility is what makes choices such as drinking an unknown potion, spending a last consumable or betting on the odds into real decisions ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 28:32](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1712); [Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 29:34](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1774); [bhauth 2020, 13:09](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=789); [Sersa Victory 2022, 28:40](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1720)).
- A death works only when the player can say why it happened and what they would do differently next time, so challenges must be understandable and each death should carry a lesson ([George Moromisato 2016, 11:08](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=668); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 2:51](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=171); [Alan Malloy 2017, 32:06](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1926); [Gillian Smith 2026, 1:06:50](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4010)).
- The time between death and the next real decision is a cost, and because permadeath means the opening is the part played most, restarts should be fast and variety should be concentrated at the start ([John Harris 2021, 17:10](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=1030); [Lisa Brown 2020, 9:28](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=568); [Andrew Aversa 2020, 13:06](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=786); [Shawn Main 2021, 17:32](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1052)).
- Permadeath is a spectrum of penalties rather than a switch, and softer modes widen the audience but have to be designed for, not just turned on, because the default mode shapes how the whole game is perceived ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 5:06](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=306); [Andrew Aversa 2020, 6:04](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=364); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 10:18](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=618); [Shawn Main 2021, 21:14](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1274); [Andrew Aversa 2020, 16:58](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1018)).
- Meta power rewards players' time ([Shawn Main 2021, 22:07](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1327)) but makes balance harder at both ends of the game, so the safer forms of meta-progression speed up the early game, widen choices, or carry knowledge and story rather than raising the power ceiling ([Jim Shepard 2017, 12:24](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=744); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 9:18](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=558); [Jim Shepard 2017, 8:11](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=491); [Arvi Teikari 2021, 28:41](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1721); [Nic Junius 2024, 24:50](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1490)).
- Randomness the player meets before deciding (setup or input randomness) feels like novelty to adapt to, while randomness that decides the result after the choice feels like losing to dice, so two teams describe moving their randomness to the input side ([Shawn Main 2017, 4:58](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=298); [Shawn Main 2017, 5:51](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=351); [Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 18:09](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1089); [David Dunham 2026, 7:06](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=426)).
- Runs are too short for luck to average out, so smooth the extremes with shuffled decks, weighted distributions, pity timers, rubber bands and top-down budgets, while keeping enough swing that the game does not go flat ([Evan Debenham 2022, 5:47](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=347); [Evan Debenham 2022, 1:39](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=99); [Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 28:59](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1739); [Brian Walker 2018, 14:00](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=840); [Shawn Main 2017, 19:57](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1197)).
- If a player with infinite patience would maximise their chance of winning by doing something tedious, the design is broken even for players who never do it, and the general cure is to make time cost something ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 0:28](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=28); [Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 5:55](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=355); [Nick McConnell 2021, 7:13](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=433); [Rosalind Miles Chapman 2020, 2:06](https://youtu.be/j9ykOdQRUQk?t=126); [Shawn Main 2021, 18:42](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1122)).
- In a single-player roguelike, let players become more powerful than their enemies, since the run reset contains broken combos, but remove any option so strong that every run must take it ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 6:45](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=405); [Courtney Liessen 2024, 11:46](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=706); [Pandamander 2024, 15:21](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=921); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 10:02](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=602); [Nic Tringali 2023, 19:17](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1157)).
- Difficulty is subjective and different players struggle with different things, so granular, clearly labelled options and unlockable tiers serve more players than one tuned setting or a single slider ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 18:16](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1096); [Philomena Schwab 2022, 7:34](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=454); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 26:46](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1606); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 2:29](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=149); [Andrea Roberts 2020, 23:25](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1405)).

## Why permadeath: consequence persistence

### Irreversibility is what makes a choice a choice

Permadeath has a bad name: it sounds like the game punishing you. Glenn Wichman, one of Rogue's authors, argues it should be called "consequence persistence". Rogue made actions irreversible not to be mean but so that its unidentified items create real decisions: if you could save, drink an unknown potion and restore when it turned out badly, the whole mystery-item mechanic would vanish. The rule is simply that once a consequence has happened it cannot be undone ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 28:32](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1712)). The panel adds the half that is easy to forget: the aim was to make the game more fun and immersive by making choices matter, and the good outcomes are just as permanent as the bad ones ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 29:34](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1774)).

Later talks converge on the same reasoning from different directions. bhauth, explaining what makes Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup good, says permadeath forces players to reason about probabilities across a huge space of possible outcomes: imagine poker with saves and reloads, and how boring it would be. Combined with random generation, permadeath makes the unknown ahead into a universe of possibility the player has to engage with, which effectively makes the game bigger. bhauth also warns it can go too far, diluting possibilities until they are not worth thinking about ([bhauth 2020, 13:09](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=789)). Sersa Victory points to a practical effect: hoarding consumables is a common habit (one Victory admits to), and the cure is situations where using them is necessary, which permadeath reinforces. In Dark Souls Victory can just retry a boss; in a tactical roguelike the threat of losing the run pressures them to teleport or pray ([Sersa Victory 2022, 28:40](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1720)).

### Tension: a long life lost to one mistake

The second thing permadeath buys is tension, and the talks describe it in strikingly similar terms. David Brevik saw turn-based play and permadeath as the source of a roguelike's tension: getting lazy, rounding a corner into an ancient multi-hued dragon with a weeks-old character at stake, palms sweating, rummaging through the backpack for any escape. That is why Brevik fought Blizzard's request to make Diablo real-time and drop permadeath ([David Brevik 2023, 6:58](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=418)). That battle was lost, but an unlockable hardcore mode in Diablo II was won; David Craddock relays a Diablo III lead developer's figure that over 300,000 of about seven million players played exclusively hardcore, and attributes the appeal to living with your consequences ([David Craddock 2016, 16:28](https://youtu.be/Gs9Nb5ZYRY0?t=988)). Todd Furmanski calls the result a precarious power narrative, clawing up to near-demigod status and then dying to one mistake, and notes how naturally it fits arcade design, where a long session can end on one wrong move; without save-reloading the player keeps a sense of tension, choice and escalation ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 4:47](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=287)). Phillip Daigle made the party RPG Rogue's Gate a roguelike for exactly this tension ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 6:15](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=375)).

The tension produces an emotional arc that players value. Sersa Victory names the swing from "best run ever" to "no way out of this mess", driven by the player's own choices, as one of the most entertaining parts of traditional roguelikes ([Sersa Victory 2022, 10:59](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=659)). Noah Swartz describes playing 30-hour NetHack games as a long arc of elation and despair, and ties that to permadeath and the hunger clock: you cannot wander forever, so there are real consequences ([Noah Swartz 2021, 9:21](https://youtu.be/IVDN5GDTIvY?t=561)). Lisa Brown finds the same drama even in turn-based Slay the Spire and Loot Rascals: lethality is high, there are no free fights, and any enemy, even a maggot, can be dangerous ([Lisa Brown 2020, 9:00](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=540)).

Harshness also keeps players coming back rather than driving them off. George Moromisato observes that NetHack's frequent "stupid deaths" create an illusion of winnability: the player always knows exactly why they died and believes next time they won't be stupid, so NetHack's addictive cry is "one more game" where Civilization's is "one more turn" ([George Moromisato 2016, 11:08](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=668)). Santiago Zapata reads Rogue's unusually harsh difficulty, which became a genre staple, as a way of making the simple journey its automated Dungeon Master creates more interesting; Zapata cites a player who has tried to beat original Rogue for four or five years ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 12:29](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=749)). Younès Rabii finds the same pull in the fan-made Pokemon Glitch, where crash-triggering NPCs and Pokemon Centers that trap you inside turn the save system into de facto permadeath ([Younès Rabii 2021, 4:56](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=296)); the game is hostile and broken, yet that hostility pushes players to see it through to the end ([Younès Rabii 2021, 9:45](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=585)).

### What permadeath means: the philosophical readings

Several speakers read permadeath as something closer to a statement about life. James Cartlidge argues it brings games closer to an authentic confrontation with mortality, because the threat of death shapes every moment-to-moment decision rather than just ending play, unlike most big-budget games where death is a checkpoint restart ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 28:05](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=1685)). Max Sahin, drawing on behavioural science, says reminders of mortality make experiences more meaningful, and roguelikes evoke fear divorced from real danger, the edge where people feel alive ([Max Sahin 2025, 7:54](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=474)).

> Permadeath changes what parts of a game are carrying the meaning-making load. — [Max Sahin 2025, 7:54](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=474)

Alexandra Leonhart connects permadeath to Halberstam's "queer art of failure": games that eject players for mistakes might be expected to deter them, yet players accept the challenge and become more involved in the world, with turn-based play leaving room to contemplate (or wallow) between turns ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:13:39](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=29619)). Max Kreminski sees permadeath as the genre's end-run around the disposability problem of generative games: by making players attached to their character, it gives a generated, replaceable hero weight ([Max Kreminski 2018, 15:58](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=958)). Younès Rabii finds the same weight in the novel La Horde du Contrevent, where each horde member trains a lifetime for a unique role, so a death removes a crucial skill for the rest of the journey as well as wounding the group emotionally ([Younès Rabii 2022, 5:21](https://youtu.be/6ik6jB2YhZg?t=321)). Nick Cummings, half joking, calls baseball's "error" statistic roguelike because it keeps every mistake on a player's permanent record, and roguelikes are the games best at haunting you with your mistakes ([Nick Cummings 2026, 51:57](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=3117)).

### What permadeath does: the practical readings

Next to these sit plainer design benefits. Arvi Teikari says permadeath made Noita's destructive powers self-balancing: players get enormous destruction but can easily kill themselves with it, and dying hilariously is part of the fun, which turned a balance problem into a feature ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 25:25](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1525)). Dan Recht notes that because a run can be restarted, a roguelike gives repeated, directed practice at hard trade-offs where the stakes feel high but no real harm is done ([Dan Recht 2017, 5:10](https://youtu.be/FnJxkId-1eE?t=310)).

### The run as one whole challenge

Permadeath also defines the shape of play. droqen calls it the "monolithic challenge": you always start from the beginning and try to master one whole task, unlike episodic games played chapter by chapter. Arcade games with limited lives had this feeling, and as that faded roguelikes carried the torch ([droqen 2020, 4:37](https://youtu.be/6Whz8bvjAKo?t=277)). The feeling does not require procedural generation: Dark Souls, with fixed enemy layouts and unforgiving runs, captures a glimmer of it as a singular task you repeat until solved ([droqen 2020, 6:11](https://youtu.be/6Whz8bvjAKo?t=371)). Julian Day adds that the run structure normalises extreme difficulty and expected failure, because there is always another run; Day has played thousands of ADOM games, won four, never won NetHack, "but who cares" ([Julian Day 2020, 15:23](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=923)).

**The test for your game.** List the decisions that exist only because they cannot be undone: drinking the unknown potion, spending the last teleport, pressing on rather than retreating. If that list is short, permadeath is adding cost without adding meaning, and the rest of this chapter's tools (fairness, restart speed, softer penalties) matter even more ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 28:32](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1712); [bhauth 2020, 13:09](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=789)).

## Fair deaths and deaths that teach

### The player has to believe the death was theirs

Permadeath works only when the player accepts the death as their own. The definitions offered in the talks converge. Moromisato's "one more game" pull, described above, depends on the player knowing exactly why they died and believing they could have avoided it ([George Moromisato 2016, 11:08](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=668)). Andrew Aversa gives Tangledeep three criteria for good difficulty: challenges are understandable, the player feels responsible for their death, and the effects of their actions are clear. The contrast Aversa draws is between dying after knowingly drinking from a fountain that might set you on fire and stepping on an invisible trap you had no way to know about. A monster's danger can be signalled by its name alone (dragon versus kobold), an identified healing potion should do something predictable, and hidden mechanics that require a wiki on another screen are bad difficulty ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 2:51](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=171)). Alan Malloy, asked how Crawl's developers judge a fun death, says there is no metric, but a fun death has a tactical lesson: something interesting the player could have done. Deaths with no good reason, or that only grinding (casting fireball at a wall 80 times) would have prevented, are not fun ([Alan Malloy 2017, 32:06](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1926)).

Aversa separates three axes that are often confused: simple versus complex, easy versus hard, good versus bad. A game can be simple yet hard without artificial difficulty such as grinding gates (slay a thousand boars before the boss) or frame-perfect execution; Aversa wanted Tangledeep's progress to come from players' skill and decisions rather than the random number generator ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 4:54](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=294)).

Gillian Smith adds the emotional condition: failure is only fun when it is normalised, when players can name what they carry away from it, ideally with a good story attached. Roguelikes do this, where higher education talks about learning through failure without making it feel okay; Smith's department made a "failure wall" of post-it notes and burned them at the end of term ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:06:50](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4010)). Andrea Interguglielmi builds Nauticrawl's core loop on the same idea: dying is part of experimenting, the player carries knowledge forward, and new lore scraps and controls restart the cycle of discovery ([Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 6:04](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=364)). Even a lost run carries something: Harry Solomons notes that the "I almost had it that time" feeling of any failed run, such as a great Balatro-style joker combination ruined by an unlucky draw, is itself something roguelikes are well equipped to make players feel ([Harry Solomons 2024, 13:14](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=794)).

### Levers for removing unfair deaths

The practical work is finding the deaths that teach nothing and removing or blunting them. Several teams describe doing exactly that:

- **Track instant kills as a design metric.** Even while embracing randomness, the Noita team actively limited instant-kill situations, tracking each new addition's effect on "insta-kill cleanliness" on an office design board ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 25:53](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1553)).
- **Wound instead of kill.** In Ultimate ADOM, Thomas Biskup made non-interactive deaths rarer: a reasonably healthy character hit by a trap is reduced to low hit points so the situation feels critical, but does not die. Biskup calls these hidden "cheat mechanisms" a way of allowing "fair dying" ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 29:28](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1768)).
- **Add undo where the game is really a puzzle.** Colin Liotta's roguelike levels for the 2017 MIT Mystery Hunt only became puzzles rather than "an endless pile of frustration" once Z to undo was added, after internal testing taught the team not to be too evil, odd as that sounds for a roguelike ([Colin Liotta 2018, 13:39](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=819)). Liotta targeted an average solve time of about two hours, hard but not impossible, and live data showed it landing there ([Colin Liotta 2018, 14:27](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=867)).
- **Change rules that produce repeated, unanswerable losses.** Chogue first copied Rogue's rule that rooms go dark when you leave, which let a roaming queen capture piece after piece each time the player re-entered; Jonathan Lessard describes how the team made rooms stay visible once revealed, a compromise that became a hallmark of the game ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 17:26](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=1046)).
- **Trim excess randomness and add warnings.** bhauth's bcrawl variant shortens maximum paralysis, replaces shaft traps, reworks boring enemies, and helps newcomers with danger warnings and a multiple-lives mode ([bhauth 2020, 22:00](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=1320)).
- **Give the player a paid way out.** In Bjarke Alexander Larsen's Telegrams from the Quiet Train, randomly corrupted logic puzzles are not guaranteed solvable. Instead, players can report a puzzle as impossible and pay a fee, justified in the fiction, to have another company solve it. It costs part of the reward but feels much better than being stuck, and doubles as an opt-out for players who don't want the puzzles at all ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 14:48](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=888)). Playtesting also showed that truly unsolvable puzzles were rarer than feared, because crisscrossing databases usually left a probable answer ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 14:02](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=842)).
- **Turn a random penalty into a dilemma.** Sersa Victory suggests that after a failure (a trap, a cursed item, a wrong answer) the player choose what to give up, as in Victory's mock-up of a Balrog whose fire burns the scroll the player picks. The penalty becomes an agonising decision instead of dice ([Sersa Victory 2022, 20:11](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1211)).

> If you are rather healthy and get hit by the trap, you won't die. Full stop. — [Thomas Biskup 2019, 29:28](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1768)

### Alternatives: expect unfairness, or make harshness the point

Not every designer removes unfair deaths. Mike Cook, working on games that generate their own rules, argues that if your generator may produce broken or unfair rules you can design around it so that winning every run is not expected: Bad Chess scores wins and losses, and roguelike streaks reward consistency across runs. Cook cites a Slay the Spire streamer who loses most games even when playing well and cares instead about playing their best in the conditions given ([Mike Cook 2023, 21:06](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1266)). Nic Tringali went further with The Banished Vault, where mistakes are punished quickly and sharply with knock-on effects across the player's whole state. The team discovered that hostility emerging from the game and leaned into it with a gothic, austere aesthetic, while acknowledging hostility is not inherently good and does not work for everyone ([Nic Tringali 2023, 7:17](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=437)). The cautionary case is Moria: Zapata says its development was guided by keeping the game challenging for a small core of players, which made it inaccessible to newcomers and contributed to it not surviving into the 1990s ([Santiago Zapata 2022, 8:59](https://youtu.be/y6WCq0jYbHo?t=539)). The choice depends on whether your audience shares the mindset Cook describes, and whether your theme can carry the harshness Tringali uses.

### Attrition: deaths decided long before they happen

Some unfair deaths are not sudden at all. Nicholas Feinberg warns that removing regeneration lets mistakes accumulate until the character is "as good as dead" long before it dies, and the player is just going through the motions. This hits fuzzier designs like Crawl or DoomRL, which assume some damage per fight, harder than tight designs like Sproggiwood or Crypt of the NecroDancer; Feinberg likes no-regeneration designs but says they are no cure-all ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 17:22](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=1042)). The same persistence has an upside that Shawn Main describes: when health carries across fights, even easy enemies matter, because the question becomes how many five-damage hits you can afford ([Shawn Main 2021, 16:29](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=989)). Persistent damage is a good source of tension only while the player can still see a way back. The section on clocks, later in this chapter, follows the same problem from the other side: what happens when a designer removes regeneration to stop players resting, and how fixed turn limits produce their own living-dead games.

### Presenting death so it lands well

How a death is framed changes how it is received. Kawa contrasts roguelike players, who expect frequent death as normal, with N++ playtesters so distressed by dying that the developers made an attract screen showing the ninja dying over and over, to signal that death is normal; Kawa argues death is core enough to deserve deliberate design attention ([Various 2018, 9:55](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=595)). Ben McGraw collects other treatments: Super Meat Boy replays all of a level's recorded attempts simultaneously after you beat it, turning the deaths into a spectacle of exploding Meat Boys ([Ben McGraw 2017, 6:42](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=402)); Dungeons of Dredmor uses a mocking death screen and achievements for common early deaths, such as dying by kicking down a door, though McGraw cautions that good humour is hard to write and the same gag wears thin ([Ben McGraw 2017, 4:45](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=285)). Jim Shepard frames death in Dungeonmans as heroic: when a hero dies, a stronger one arrives from the academy, and players usually win by throwing heroes at evil until it gives up. Shepard wanted heroic deaths, "Boromir style", not deaths from starving ([Jim Shepard 2016, 7:13](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=433)). And Aversa points out that because players expect to die often, a fair but silly death, like being headbutted into lava by a frog and then surrounded by more frogs, can still be a good story ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 5:47](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=347)).

**In practice.** Audit every way your game can kill the player. For each, ask: was there a warning the player could read (a name, a sound, a visible tile)? Was there counterplay available at the time? Will the player be able to name what they would do differently? Where the answer is no, choose a lever: remove it, wound instead of kill, add a warning, add an out, or, if harshness is the point, design scoring and framing so players don't expect to win every run ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 2:51](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=171); [Alan Malloy 2017, 32:06](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1926); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 29:28](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1768); [Mike Cook 2023, 21:06](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1266)).

## The cost of starting over: restarts, run length and the early game

### Death-to-play time is a design budget

If players are meant to learn by dying, every second between death and the next interesting decision is a cost. John Harris puts it in poker terms: time invested in a run is the ante, and dying loses it all, so the longer a roguelike takes to start, the worse it is. Advanced Rogue 5 rolls your stats so you can start in under a second; Advanced Rogue 7 adds character creation and a mandatory trading post and is slower ([John Harris 2021, 17:10](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=1030)). Lisa Brown measured it: Nuclear Throne gets you back into play in about five seconds, Enter the Gungeon took over ten, and that slower failure loop is, for Brown, one reason Gungeon did not stick. Celeste gives just enough time to register the mistake before you are back in action ([Lisa Brown 2020, 9:28](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=568)). Ben McGraw singles out Spelunky's extremely low death penalty, jumping straight back in, as one of the best things about its opening, and suggests games without character builds should lean on it ([Ben McGraw 2017, 5:40](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=340)).

### Permadeath promises that the early game will be seen many times

Andrew Aversa's "End of Permadeath" talk turns this into a content argument. Plot time in a run against content seen and permadeath produces a pyramid wide at the bottom: the opening is played far more than anything else. Default permadeath therefore promises variety in starts, monsters, locations and character creation; players who expect to die and get the same five floors get bored and leave negative reviews ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 13:06](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=786)). Aversa's conclusion is a test: include permadeath only if you can fulfil the promise of a fun, varied early game without a heavy opening story. If the experience you want to deliver is the epic late game, players should reach it sooner, and permadeath perhaps should not be the default ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 24:30](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1470)).

> We should think about why we are including permadeath in the game and if we are willing to fulfill the promise. — [Andrew Aversa 2020, 24:30](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1470)

Benjamin Berman gives a tuning rule for that opening: the start of every life should be winnable by playing randomly, because a player who knows nothing behaves indistinguishably from random input. Close your eyes, press random keys; if you reach level 2, early difficulty is tuned ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 17:46](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1066)). The opening still matters for skilled players: bhauth notes that for a strong DCSS player on a win streak, the simpler early game is the most dangerous part, so streakers play it very carefully ([bhauth 2020, 22:48](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=1368)).

Variety at the start is mostly about where the run begins. Shawn Main argues for enforced, distinct starting positions: NetHack's classes with randomised stats, Lab of Legends' champions with very different decks, Hades' first-room boon ([Shawn Main 2021, 17:32](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1052)). Caves of Qud replaced its single fixed starting village with a choice of four regions, each granting reputation with particular factions (start in the marsh and insects and fish like you more) ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 11:47](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=707)). Even a small shuffle helps: Hannah Blair Salzman found Shovel Knight's final boss rush tolerable to repeat because the bosses come in no fixed order, so dying on the last one wasn't frustrating ([Hannah Blair Salzman 2022, 6:05](https://youtu.be/6GSXaM1PTMg?t=365)). Some genres resist this: the Against the Storm developers say a city builder's basic actions (roads, wood camp, gathering camp) are long enough that some repetition at the start of every run is hard to avoid, even after heavy work on variety ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 11:14](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=674)).

### Run length as a lever

Run length sets how much each death costs, and teams that name a target early report it as a fixed point for other decisions. The spectrum in the talks runs:

- **Espresso, 2-3 minutes.** Lee Tusman's One Dimensional Dungeon is a run aimed at a high score, shorter than a coffee break ([Lee Tusman 2020, 8:47](https://youtu.be/-e4gF_SKWPk?t=527)).
- **Coffee break, about 10-20 minutes.** John Harris describes Strange Adventures in Infinite Space as a full game in about 20 minutes if you don't die ([John Harris 2016, 5:54](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=354)). Desktop Dungeons, Danny Day explains, was Rodain Joubert's attempt to compress the feeling of a long Stone Soup run into a ten-minute single-screen session, cutting resting and food so every action is a meaningful choice ([Danny Day 2018, 0:48](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=48)). Peglin's demo was one 20-minute act, tuned so genre-experienced players would win on the second or third try, and over 30,000 players replayed it for more than three hours ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 7:22](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=442)).
- **Movie length, 60-120 minutes.** Phillip Daigle took FTL's complete experience in about an hour and a half as a deliberate goal for Rogue's Gate ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 7:17](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=437)). David Dunham chose roguelike structure for Thousand Hells to deliver procedural narrative in runs of an hour to an hour and a half, closer to a movie than a novel trilogy ([David Dunham 2026, 5:57](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=357)). Against the Storm set a 1.5-2 hour target early and balanced every major change against it ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 24:41](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1481)).

Length is tuned, not just chosen. Casey Yano says Slay the Spire's acts shrank from 17 floors to 16 and eventually 13, partly because the developers were tired of replaying act 1 ([Casey Yano 2022, 12:57](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=777)). Shorter levels inside a run help too: Todd Furmanski describes Dragon's Descent's short, variable-difficulty levels as a "potato chip" compulsion, reinforced by more points for going deeper ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 9:41](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=581)).

Length also scales the sting. Aversa notes that losing a 10-15 hour run hurts far more than losing a coffee-break roguelike or a board game, and the average session length changes how players feel about a spike that takes 80% of their health ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 28:22](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1702)). The Against the Storm team wanted the roguelike rhythm where you play two hours, leave for two weeks, then play eight, with decisions that have repercussions ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 6:12](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=372)).

### Short runs and short horizons serve particular players

Two speakers make the case that short runs are an access issue as well as a pacing one. Lisa Brown, who scores low on strategy motivation, says roguelikes work for them because of short, visible time horizons: decisions pay off quickly and progress is legible (Nuclear Throne shows how close you got, Slay the Spire lays out the map, Loot Rascals has five clear sections), while long-horizon games and even Into the Breach's several-moves-ahead planning bounced off Brown ([Lisa Brown 2020, 15:12](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=912)). Because they gain power only to complete the task at hand, short runs and frequent clean slates mean failure doesn't sting even when they die a lot ([Lisa Brown 2020, 19:40](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1180)). Hannah Blair Salzman found that short, self-contained runs could hold attention through poor mental health when 300-hour open-world games could not, even when more total hours ended up going into the roguelike ([Hannah Blair Salzman 2022, 4:16](https://youtu.be/6GSXaM1PTMg?t=256)).

**In practice.** Measure the seconds from death to the next real decision and cut them ([Lisa Brown 2020, 9:28](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=568)). Set a run-length target early and check major changes against it ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 24:41](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1481)). Put your variety budget at the front of the run, where permadeath guarantees it will be seen ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 13:06](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=786)), and test that a player pressing random keys survives the first stretch ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 17:46](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1066)).

## Softening death: a spectrum of penalties

### Not a switch but a spectrum, and the default matters most

Andrew Aversa redefines optional permadeath as any mode where dying does not necessarily cost all progress. That covers partial losses (keep some things, lose weapons or experience), lives, saves, rewinds and checkpoints; it is a spectrum, not an on/off switch ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 5:06](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=306)). Before any balance question, the default matters: citing opt-in versus opt-out organ donation studies, Aversa argues that the default mode and how the permadeath option is presented on the title screen and in character creation shape how players perceive and play the game ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 6:04](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=364)).

> How we define the default experience of a game as developers is monumentally important and affects how the game is perceived. — [Andrew Aversa 2020, 6:04](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=364)

### The case for softer modes

The evidence for offering them is substantial. About 30% of Tangledeep's players choose its non-permadeath adventure mode, where dying costs experience, job points and gold, including some of its most dedicated players; it lets far more people see content that only around 2% of runs reach, and they then share encounters and builds that motivate hardcore players. Aversa included it as an explicitly "casual" concession, reasoning that players could save-scum anyway ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 10:18](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=618)). Michael Langford recommends optional no-permadeath or easier modes for less proficient players such as children, as Son of a Witch offers: permadeath keeps the game at the child's level, but an option lets them see the rest ([Michael Langford 2021, 15:18](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=918)). Christine Tomlinson argues that Boyfriend Dungeon's softened permadeath and cozy framing reach players who find permadeath too scary and would otherwise think roguelites are "not for me" ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 16:14](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=974)), and describes roguelites as tiers of entry: Boyfriend Dungeon as a gentle start, Hades a step up in challenge and adherence to roguelike mechanics ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 18:25](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=1105)). Philomena Schwab shows how far one toggle can move a game: turning off death in The Wandering Village makes it a chill happiness-management game, while turning off manual saving makes it harder and more roguelike ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 12:12](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=732)). Mike Cook adds a quieter benefit: without permadeath, players can return to and really get to know a generated place, noticing the fewer things that change ([Mike Cook 2026, 27:17](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1637)).

### The case against doing it carelessly

Softening without redesign causes its own problems. Shawn Main describes Lab of Legends' later version, which replaced classic permadeath with an RPG-style "keep going": without consequences for failure, players got stuck with bad choices and banged their heads against a wall, and since there was no way to grind out of trouble they had to retire runs themselves ([Shawn Main 2021, 21:14](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1274)). Aversa lists further traps. Designing equally for both modes is hard on a small budget, and a hazard acceptable with saves, such as a monster that takes half your HP or an invisible trap, draws "this is unfair, I lost my progress" reviews from permadeath players ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 16:58](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1018)). Save-anywhere is not necessarily easier than permadeath, because a player can save into an unrecoverable state deep in a dungeon without healing, which feels like an impossible puzzle rather than a heroic death ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 22:11](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1331)). And once players expect to finish, the final boss, endgame options, gear progression and story payoff all have to deliver; the example given is Diablo III's maligned story ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 15:07](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=907)). Reviews of the same permadeath structures show opposite complaints, from the early-game slog of replaying with permadeath on to 13 hours spent reaching a great endgame, which Aversa reads as a sign that design and option presentation set expectations ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 18:17](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1097)).

### Points along the spectrum

Between "lose everything" and "lose nothing", the talks describe many intermediate penalties:

- **Lives.** Aversa sees a lives system as a compromise that gives the designer room to "do a few unfair things", push limits and offer new rewards without wiping all progress on one death ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 21:05](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1265)).
- **Collapse and lose your items.** In Mystery Dungeon, John Harris explains, the character collapses on failure and is ejected without their items, usually back at level one, while successful clears let you keep items that ease later runs; each adventure is one in a series ([John Harris 2024, 11:59](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=719)).
- **One chance to recover.** In Dark Souls, Craddock notes, your souls stay in a bloodstain you get one chance to reclaim; die again and hours of farmed souls are lost, without restarting the game ([David Craddock 2016, 16:59](https://youtu.be/Gs9Nb5ZYRY0?t=1019)).
- **A mortal choice.** When a Wildermyth hero hits zero health, the player chooses: fall back maimed (losing an arm or eye, or gaining a scar) or die in a blaze of glory with a powerful final act. Death stays meaningful but uncommon in a party game spanning years ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 6:25](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=385)).
- **A reframed reset.** Andrea Roberts' Roundguard wraps death in a theatre: the host says it was just a bad run and resets the stage, and a small death token carries into the next run, not run-changing but enough to give an idea and hope ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 15:26](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=926)).
- **Ghosts and revives in multiplayer.** A networked real-time Angband variant turned dead characters into ghosts other players could revive, with permadeath only if the ghost died ([Tariq et al. 2016, 26:47](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1607)). In Tyriq Plummer's Scrubbin' Trubble only a total party wipe ends the run; fallen players return next floor at a growing score penalty, and a party in trouble can leave a level early and take the penalty together ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 17:02](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=1022)).
- **A toggle**, as in The Wandering Village above ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 12:12](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=732)).

### What the choice depends on

The choice turns on three things the talks keep returning to: who your audience is (children, cozy players, hardcore streakers), what you can afford to build and balance twice, and how long a run is, since a long run makes total loss sting more ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 28:22](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1702)). Joel Clark's warning from Blaseball applies to all of it: players have very different tolerances for chaos, so incinerating a favourite player delights some fans and upsets others, and a single experience cannot fit everyone ([Joel Clark 2020, 22:47](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1367)).

## Deaths that leave a mark: legacies, bones and worlds that remember

### The world keeps what you lose

The alternative to a clean reset is a death that feeds something persistent. Tarn Adams describes Dwarf Fortress's permadeath as the engine of the whole game: lost forts and dead adventurers are added to a persistent world you keep playing in, so as long as something persists, nothing is truly lost. That is where the "losing is fun" motto comes from; they later let players retire adventurers and forts so others can meet them as AI-controlled characters ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 15:22](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=922)).

Prey: Mooncrash made the choice explicit. Rich Wilson says the team distilled death into two models: a stateless, session-based "Spelunky model", like a sport with daily challenges, and a persistent "Rogue Legacy model", where death feeds progress toward a long-range goal. They chose the latter, adding unlockable characters and meta-progression currency ([Rich Wilson 2021, 13:36](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=816)). Five characters play in sequence through one finite-resource world until all have escaped or died, then it resets. A character who escapes with lots of loot leaves the drawers empty for later selves; one who dies is resurrected as a monster that the next self must fight to recover the gear. Wilson calls this accountability and long-range agency ([Rich Wilson 2021, 15:28](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=928)).

Cole Wehrle's board game Oath takes persistence furthest. Every in-game state is also a valid start state, so each game's ending becomes the next game's beginning, layered like paint over a picture, and the world accumulates history without any pre-written plot ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 12:15](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=735)). The rate of change is tuned: six cards leave the deck and six enter every game, about 10%, giving a generational feel over an imagined three centuries rather than a stone-age-to-spaceship leap ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 21:11](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1271)).

> Every in-game state in Oath is also a start state. — [Cole Wehrle 2025, 12:15](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=735)

### Smaller legacies

Most games persist far less, and the talks show a range of small marks a death can leave:

- **A grave with loot.** In Dungeonmans a dead hero of high enough level leaves a pyre marked with their name, where a later character may find the dropped weapon; Jim Shepard borrowed it from Rastan's game-over screen to make previous heroes part of the game's legends ([Jim Shepard 2016, 10:19](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=619)).
- **A bequest.** Ben McGraw describes a Windows 3.1-themed roguelike where a dying character bequeaths one item as a one-time gift to a future character, alongside currency that accumulates across deaths, so deaths do not feel wasted ([Ben McGraw 2017, 7:33](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=453)).
- **Bones, and the case for turning them off.** NetHack's bones files let a later game inherit a dead character's gear. Adeon plays speedruns with them off, because a dead wizard's cloak of magic resistance makes a run feel like cheating ([Adeon 2017, 23:36](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=1416)).
- **Places that improve across runs.** In the first Shiren, John Harris explains, repeatedly donating to a struggling restaurant turns it into a reliable resource and eventually unlocks a bonus dungeon ([John Harris 2024, 12:33](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=753)). Shiren 2 is meant to be run many times, gathering materials to build a castle that defends the town from the Oni before you take the fight to them ([John Harris 2024, 16:47](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=1007)).
- **People who carry the story.** Jim Shepard suggests romantic partners can provide continuity: if one dies, the other picks up the pieces, though Shepard admits this departs from permadeath ([Jim Shepard 2019, 18:41](https://youtu.be/LKCRim02opc?t=1121)). In La Horde du Contrevent, Younès Rabii reads successive hordes as runs, each trying to go further using the notebook the previous horde's scribe left where it died ([Younès Rabii 2022, 6:27](https://youtu.be/6ik6jB2YhZg?t=387)).
- **Worlds that reference earlier worlds.** In an exploration game of their own, Florence Smith Nicholls proposes feeding entries from earlier generated villages into new ones, so objects across playthroughs reference each other; each unrepeatable world is already a kind of permadeath ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2022, 9:33](https://youtu.be/IanNZxUaVQs?t=573)). Thomas Biskup's team considered treating ADOM as a prequel whose achievements unlock things in Ultimate ADOM, though porting characters directly is unlikely ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 28:01](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1681)).

### Burdens instead of upgrades?

In the Q&A after Harry Solomons' talk, the host, Alexei, raised an open question: meta-progression could invert the power fantasy, with runs accruing burdens or eerie baggage that weigh down future runs. Examples raised in the exchange include NetHack bones with your own grave and cursed items, Loop Hero's world solidifying, and Rogue Legacy reminding you it took 48 generations. Solomons warned that if each death simply makes you worse, the result is frustration; characters might instead accrue relationships to death the way spaces do ([Harry Solomons 2024, 26:17](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1577)).

**In practice.** Decide what a death should leave behind: world state, a story, an item, a place. Persisting world state and story changes what the next run is about; persisting items and power changes how hard it is. Biskup's stated aim for Ultimate ADOM, an overarching metaplot and meta-abilities with a smooth curve rather than power creep, is the line to hold ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 14:33](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=873)). Where you do carry power across, the next section's tools apply.

## Meta-progression: knowledge, power and presence

### A framework: what survives game over

Jim Shepard gives the clearest definition. A "try" is one attempt, ending when you run out of HP or similar; game over is the full reset to a state as if no one had touched the game. Metaprogression is anything that survives game over. A long between-adventures structure like Darkest Dungeon's hamlet is, in this sense, just one long try ([Jim Shepard 2017, 3:38](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=218)). Shepard sorts metaprogression into three kinds: meta knowledge, meta power and meta presence, covering knowledge first because designers rarely think of it as progression ([Jim Shepard 2017, 5:20](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=320)). Meta power itself comes in two forms. Kinetic power is direct stat boosts, so you walk out the door swinging harder than your predecessor; soft or potential power widens future choices, as when bringing back diamonds makes the shop stock a new item or unlocks a class ([Jim Shepard 2017, 8:11](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=491)).

### The core disagreement: should runs make you stronger?

The talks divide sharply on meta power. On one side, Shawn Main argues, knowingly controversial before a roguelike audience, that meta-progression pairs naturally with a roguelike core because players want to be rewarded for their time, not only through their own improving skill, pointing to Rogue Legacy and to Hades making an art of it ([Shawn Main 2021, 22:07](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1327)). Shepard adds that meta power softens the edge of permadeath, lets players try silly builds without feeling they wasted their time, and keeps more players from abandoning or refunding a game when something cool happens after death ([Jim Shepard 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=564)). Tim Keenan notes that unlocks are also a lever for run variety, since they set a direction ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:42:37](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31357)), and Brian Cronin says Monster Train's logbook of card unlocks and its escalating Covenant challenge ranks are something players particularly enjoy ([Brian Cronin 2021, 2:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=125)). Jasper Cole considers constant progress across runs an important piece of a modern roguelike, and Backpack Hero's story mode lets players bring an item back to build up the town even after losing ([Jasper Cole 2023, 25:46](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1546)).

On the other side, Arvi Teikari describes Noita's reliance on "virtual skill": players progress by increasing their knowledge rather than unlocking more powerful items, which suits dynamic emergent systems ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 28:41](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1721)). Keenan warns that meta-progression can make a game feel grindy, and purists dislike playing several runs to "get momentum going" ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:42:37](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31357)). Aversa puts the failure mode in a phrase, "I have to die to build up my character", against the version that excites, "even if I die I get to pick another starting location" ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 26:31](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1591)).

The balance problems are concrete. Shepard says meta power adds a variable to balance: too much makes the early game a boring walkover, while tuning late content for players who have died many times builds a grind wall for first-run players. Give monsters extra fangs on the assumption of 20 deaths and you force players to suicide-farm bonuses, "two different sides of a sad spectrum" between crutch and grind ([Jim Shepard 2017, 12:24](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=744)). Courtney Liessen, who embraces game-breaking combos because the run reset contains them, warns that meta unlocks must be doled out carefully so a broken state doesn't get locked in permanently, unless escalating power is designed as the path to victory ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 12:33](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=753)); Liessen's case for broken combos inside a run comes up under "Power within a run". John Harris's cautionary example is the Wii Shiren, aimed at a US audience, which kept experience levels after death: it encouraged grinding instead of making do with what you have, and Harris considers it the series' weakest ([John Harris 2024, 19:48](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=1188)). Shepard traces the darkest version back to arcades, where continues granting extra power (Shinobi's ninja magic, 1942's extra bombs) were designed to extract more quarters at the hard parts ([Jim Shepard 2017, 11:28](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=688)).

What the choice depends on: whether your systems produce enough novelty that knowledge alone keeps runs fresh (Noita's case), and whether your audience wants to feel time rewarded (Main's case). Either way, the balance cost of kinetic power is real.

### Middle paths

Most of the techniques in the talks try to give the reward without the crutch.

**Speed up the early game, don't raise the ceiling.** Aversa argues meta-progression should get the player through the early game faster rather than raise their power ceiling each run. Tangledeep's heroic mode lets you bank items and gold, plant trees and raise pets for future characters, which helps you reach the gear tier you had already found sooner; skills and experience do not transfer. Aversa contrasts this with Rogue Legacy-style progression where a found sword only benefits the next character after death, and says players mostly liked the Tangledeep approach ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 9:18](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=558)).

> Rather than using meta progress to increase our power little by little with each run, instead let's use this to just get the player through the early game sooner. — [Andrew Aversa 2018, 9:18](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=558)

**Unlocks that only change probabilities.** Dan Recht notes that Dream Quest's meta-progression is an achievement system whose rewards are new cards appearing in the game, so even between runs the player only manipulates the odds, the same way in-run growth works ([Dan Recht 2017, 6:12](https://youtu.be/FnJxkId-1eE?t=372)). This is Shepard's soft power in its purest form ([Jim Shepard 2017, 8:11](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=491)).

**Unlocks that change the rules.** Andrea Roberts' Roundguard gives post-victory relics that each alter a core rule (status effects, enemy responses, map generation, gravity) and can be stacked freely, letting players reshape the game rather than simply overpower it ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 21:27](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1287)). The section on difficulty settings returns to Roundguard's unlocks as a way of tuning challenge.

**Cap the carry-over and preserve a later test.** Dungeonmans caps carried-over gear, usually a few stat points and slightly better gear for early confidence, and makes later enemies deal escalating elemental damage that stats alone cannot absorb, so mitigation must be found in the world; an Ironman mode has no carry-over at all ([Jim Shepard 2017, 27:39](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1659)).

**Give content, not power.** Shepard imagines meta presence used for pity: an NPC who has watched your pile of dead characters hands you a ticket to a new dungeon, giving struggling players new content free of power creep ([Jim Shepard 2017, 25:38](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1538)).

**Knowledge as progression.** Stella Mazeika describes randomizer players progressing across seeds through deeper base-game knowledge, randomizer-specific knowledge, routing and glitch techniques, such as an instakill spell that exiles Lich in Final Fantasy ([Stella Mazeika 2019, 8:43](https://youtu.be/C7laugXEc9s?t=523)).

**Story that advances on every run.** Nic Junius argues that braided narratives ease the sting of a lost run, because almost every run advances someone's side story; in Hades, at minimum, you get to chat with a denizen of the House. Players also trigger story beats in different places and compare notes ([Nic Junius 2024, 24:50](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1490)).

**Make progress visible in the world.** Tabea Iseli's Grimoire Groves presents unlocks as plants placed in an overgrown garden at the home base, with the spell tree a literal tree, so the garden shows what the player can do; players loved it and wanted to place things freely ([Tabea Iseli 2024, 4:16](https://youtu.be/-MX1imoSxTg?t=256)). Befriending shop NPCs through mini games gives extra shop choices and discounts, lets them move into your forest, and helps in boss fights staged in their backyards ([Tabea Iseli 2024, 7:38](https://youtu.be/-MX1imoSxTg?t=458)). Backpack Hero's town is another diegetic store of progress ([Jasper Cole 2023, 25:46](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1546)).

### Choosing which loop carries progress

Gillian Smith offers a frame for placing all of this. Roguelikes structure experience as fractal progression loops, moment to moment, room to room, run to run, and meta across games, which mirror each other and hold each other in tension, unlike the linear, backward-designed progression of a curriculum ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:05:20](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=3920)). Read with Shepard's three kinds, the design question is which loop each kind of progress belongs to: power you want felt within a run belongs in the run loop; knowledge accumulates in the player whether you design for it or not; and whatever you put in the meta loop, whether power, presence or story, should change what the next run is like without deciding it before it starts.

## What randomness is for

Permadeath is what makes a roguelike's randomness matter: a bad roll cannot be reloaded away ([bhauth 2020, 13:09](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=789)). The next five sections turn from death itself to the forces inside a run that decide it, starting with randomness. Before you tame randomness you should know what it is buying you. The talks give three answers that reinforce each other: randomness produces variety, it produces drama, and it produces uncertainty, which is what makes a game worth playing again.

### Variety, replay and uncertainty

In a talk on randomness, Shawn Main calls this the biggest point: randomness creates variety, and variety multiplies how long players stay engaged, because the more possible experiences a game offers the more total time players will spend in it ([Shawn Main 2017, 3:27](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=207)). Evan Debenham's talk on Shattered Pixel Dungeon opens from the same place: randomness is what makes roguelikes replayable ([Evan Debenham 2022, 1:25](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=85)). Zach and Tarn Adams tell the history version. Replaying a fixed adventure such as King's Quest made no sense because you knew what would happen; roguelikes answered that problem because procedural generation made the treasures, enemies and dungeon different every time, and with permadeath and a high-score list it kept them playing Rogue until the floppy disk wore out ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 3:05](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=185)).

The deeper claim is that what a game needs is uncertainty, and randomness is only one way to get it. Main says the answer to "do games need randomness?" is obviously no, but they do need a source of uncertainty: nobody plays tic-tac-toe, while rock-paper-scissors works because the opponent's choice is unknown, and Main will not replay Portal because every puzzle is already known ([Shawn Main 2017, 13:43](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=823)). A Magic: The Gathering designer in the 2016 lightning talks made the same argument, saying their reputation for liking randomness is really a love of large possibility spaces: games that do not test physical skill need uncertainty to create drama, and explicit randomness is the most common historical source of it but not the only one ([Tariq et al. 2016, 4:03](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=243)).

Randomness also serves particular player motives. Lisa Brown lists improvisation and surprise among the reasons for liking roguelikes: a relic picked up mid-run in Slay the Spire that forces you to rethink the whole build is a satisfying experiment ([Lisa Brown 2020, 11:59](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=719)). Joel Clark calls randomness, procedural generation included, the cheapest form of chaos you can add to a game, and says Blaseball openly embraces being "an RNG with lore on top" because players cannot understand randomness and that is what makes it exciting ([Joel Clark 2020, 8:32](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=512)). Main adds drama: a roll at a decisive moment spins the story in a new direction, whether it is leaning in to see a critical success in an RPG or a big poker bet paying off, and roguelikes share that moment ([Shawn Main 2017, 3:54](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=234)). Even the early-game luck of traditional roguelikes, such as meeting potion-gated puzzles before you can identify any potions, is described as part of their pull; sometimes you get an overpowered run very early, and that is fascinating ([Qristy Overton 2021, 13:49](https://youtu.be/zlJNIJOog9M?t=829)).

### Setup randomness and results randomness

The most useful distinction in this material is Main's split between two places randomness can sit. *Setup randomness* happens before the player decides: the map, the starting position, the starting characters are generated, and then the player adapts with real choices, as in Spelunky and roguelikes generally. It offers novelty rather than frustration ([Shawn Main 2017, 4:58](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=298)). *Results randomness* happens after the player decides: they act, and a roll decides the outcome. It produces the highest emotion, and it is also where players say "damn it, I lost to a roll of the dice." Main treats the two as ends of a spectrum: Magic randomises the opening hand (setup), but each turn's draw can leave you needing one specific card, which is intensely emotional and makes people swear at the game ([Shawn Main 2017, 5:51](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=351)).

Setup randomness need not reduce skill; it can test more of it. Main's example is Fischer Random Chess, which shuffles the back row so that players must improvise instead of reciting memorised openings, set against Richard Garfield's joke of rolling a die after checkmate, which adds uncertainty while testing nothing ([Shawn Main 2017, 9:01](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=541)).

Two teams arrived at the same move independently: keep the randomness, but shift it from the result to the input. Justin Ma and Matthew Davis say Into the Breach did not take randomness out so much as change how it is presented. Enemy setup and spawns are random, but the player's own actions are deterministic, like dice games where you roll seven dice first and then decide how to use them, which feels far less random than rolling to see whether you hit; Ma names this input versus output randomness ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 18:09](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1089)). It was partly a reaction to FTL, where evasion rolls and shop luck make runs swing like a slot machine between an amazing setup and never finding a shop. For Into the Breach, squads were designed to be self-sufficient without weapon drops and enemy attacks are predicted ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 14:23](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=863)). David Dunham made the same switch for Thousand Hells: King of Dragon Pass and Six Ages resolved tasks with opaque dice, players complained they didn't know what was going on, so Thousand Hells resolves them with a shuffled deck the player can see, built from the characters' abilities ([David Dunham 2026, 7:06](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=426)).

Andrea Roberts widens the idea further. Roundguard fires its hero from a ballista to bounce through the dungeon like Peggle, and that physics stands in for what other games express as percent chance to hit or evade; RNG still drives dungeon generation, loot and item procs ([Andrea Roberts 2019, 2:06](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=126)). The physics is fully deterministic (a cranked-up aim predictor shows the hero follows the line exactly), yet after a few bounces the outcome is a mess in players' heads, like Plinko. Roberts proposes calling any system too complicated for players to model a *system of uncertainty*, a broader tool than random number generation ([Andrea Roberts 2019, 3:05](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=185)).

> It's a system of uncertainty, which really is any system that is that complicated that we can't model it out. — [Andrea Roberts 2019, 3:05](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=185)

Roundguard does not secretly correct bounces; its only intervention is slowing time at dramatic moments such as near misses so the player can react ([Andrea Roberts 2019, 12:50](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=770)).

### Drama or gambling: the line between them

The talks agree that losing to randomness hurts, and Main pins down why: the feeling of powerlessness. The test is whether a player reviewing their choices at the end concludes they did everything right and it was just the roll ([Shawn Main 2017, 10:43](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=643)). From there the positions diverge.

Main defends big swings. Highs and lows are powerful; games that smooth out all uncertainty often become a flat exercise in micro-optimisation, so the goal is to keep the variance while making sure the player still has agency and the game does not feel like it is playing the player ([Shawn Main 2017, 19:57](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1197)). Dylan Gedig takes a similar bet with Peglin, which ties map navigation to its pachinko aiming so that a flubbed shot can send a streamer down an unplanned route. Gedig admits players and reviewers criticise the lack of agency, but argues it creates memorable adapt-on-the-fly moments, and the map nodes themselves are static and learnable ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 25:03](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1503)).

John Harris marks the far end. A random dungeon with no meaningful structure reduces to gambling: you progress through encounters you barely control, and the only real choice is whether to press on or stop. Harris's examples are a Flash game built on the AD&D random dungeon appendix, which plays as a simulation of whether to keep exploring or bank your funds, and the PLATO game dnd, where a first-level character has about a 50% chance of dying in every fight until finding a magic item ([John Harris 2016, 14:03](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=843)). An audience member at the talk supplied the test that separates the two. Artful randomness creates problems players can build intuition for but never fully solve by logic, the way no Go player can read out every future; poor randomness produces events that no intuition can learn, and that is gambling rather than a game. Harris agreed ([John Harris 2016, 29:20](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1760)).

That test reconciles Main and Harris better than splitting the difference does. A big swing is fine when the player could have seen it coming in principle and planned for it; it becomes gambling when nothing the player learns changes the odds.

### Variance is an audience choice

How much variance to allow depends on who is playing and what they want. Main points out that more randomness lets players of very different skill play together: Main could play Magic against one of the world's best and have a decent shot, whereas playing a chess grandmaster would mean being walked over ([Shawn Main 2017, 12:35](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=755)). Gavin Verhey describes Magic doing this on purpose. Land draws and mana problems give built-in variance, and a strong early rare can let a newer player upset a veteran, but never every time, because the experienced player has invested a lot ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 15:10](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=910)). The right level differs by audience even within one game: Commander players want big swings and wild outcomes because the point is having fun, while competitive limited is tuned for moderate variance ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 48:14](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=2894)). Verhey also distinguishes visible from hidden variance. Wizards avoids making a coin-flip card strong because that luck is "in your face": in player-versus-player play the loser rages that the opponent "hit". Verhey suggests such face-up "bingo" effects may be more fun in player-versus-environment play ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 15:54](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=954)), which is most roguelikes.

Dan Recht draws a player-side lesson from Dream Quest: once you accept uncertainty, you can make your own luck by drawing more cards (making more attempts) and by stacking the deck (improving what you draw from) ([Dan Recht 2017, 8:19](https://youtu.be/FnJxkId-1eE?t=499)). A design that offers both levers gives the player agency over randomness without removing it.

### Players misread probability

Whatever you choose, your players will judge it with poor intuitions. Nicholas Feinberg says roguelike developers meet the same misunderstandings again and again: missing five attacks in a row, or rare gold dragon armour turning up on the third floor in back-to-back games, feels broken, and the developer usually has to answer that the game is probably not broken ([Nicholas Feinberg 2020, 3:41](https://youtu.be/GMkBT4UbvAs?t=221)). Johnathon Pagnutti gives designers the maths to reason past that intuition. Repeated percentage rolls, such as Fire Emblem: Three Houses stat growths or a run of XCOM shots, follow a binomial distribution, which you can read as the chance of exactly n successes or as the cumulative chance of n or fewer. The cumulative curve is a sigmoid that flattens at the top, so for a favourable coin the chance of 16 or fewer successes out of 20 is nearly the same as the chance of 20 or fewer ([Johnathon Pagnutti 2026, 9:01](https://youtu.be/DbZe8rWviS0?t=541)). One consequence is counter-intuitive: when the odds favour the player, the best case is always more likely than the worst. With a 60% growth rate, Edelgard is far more likely to gain strength on all six of her levels as a Fighter than on none ([Johnathon Pagnutti 2026, 10:09](https://youtu.be/DbZe8rWviS0?t=609)). Combining the exact and cumulative curves lets you say how lucky or unlucky a character's actual total is at a given level (16 strength after ten Noble levels is well behind the curve, 20 is ahead), though Pagnutti admits that chaining classes by assuming the median outcome of the previous one is a fudge ([Johnathon Pagnutti 2026, 10:40](https://youtu.be/DbZe8rWviS0?t=640)).

### Deciding where randomness sits

Taken together, these talks suggest a sequence of questions. First, where does your uncertainty come from: dice, a deck, hidden information, or a deterministic system too complex to model ([Andrea Roberts 2019, 3:05](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=185); [David Dunham 2026, 7:06](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=426))? Second, for each random element, is it setup or result? Setup randomness asks the player to adapt; results randomness asks them to accept. Move a roll to the input side when its swing is large and the player could not have planned for it ([Shawn Main 2017, 5:51](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=351); [Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 18:09](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1089)). Third, apply the intuition test: can a player who has died to this fifty times play better against it on the fifty-first ([John Harris 2016, 29:20](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1760))? Fourth, decide how much variance your audience wants, and whether weaker players should be able to win sometimes ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 48:14](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=2894); [Shawn Main 2017, 12:35](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=755)). The next section covers what to do with the randomness you keep.

## Smoothing the sharp edges of RNG

### The problem: short runs, many outliers

Debenham names the "sharp edges" of RNG: missing constantly, rolling minimum damage, enemies hitting for maximum every time, items that do not suit the build, the same item type over and over, stronger enemies arriving together. At worst players feel at the mercy of the RNG, with success decided by luck rather than skill ([Evan Debenham 2022, 1:25](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=85)). Roguelikes suffer from these extremes more than most games, because a single run is too short for outcomes to converge to the average while players play many runs and so meet the outliers. A 1-in-10 chance comes up twice in a row 1 time in 100, and occasionally takes more than 40 tries ([Evan Debenham 2022, 5:47](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=347)). Debenham defines smoothing as cutting those extremes while keeping enough randomness that the game stays exciting and the player still feels in control ([Evan Debenham 2022, 1:39](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=99)).

Sébastien Benard of Dead Cells goes further: "randomly generated" should mean random in a controlled way, because full randomness mostly produces chaotic, uninteresting results; in that sense the claim of random levels is "a lie" ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 26:43](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1603)). Benard frames this as a *hidden game master*. A tabletop GM fudges dice to create the illusion that the chaos was intended, and the Left 4 Dead director watches the players and adjusts. In the same way, game code can observe the run, notice that the player is short of money or behind the economy, and drop something, because the perceived experience matters more than the raw results. Thinking of each tool as "acknowledge a situation and fix it" helps you design it efficiently ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 31:42](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1902)).

Neither speaker says you must smooth. Debenham closes by saying it is fine to keep RNG sharp: Shattered Pixel Dungeon prizes consistency, another game may prefer more randomness, and these are tools to choose from ([Evan Debenham 2022, 13:11](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=791)). Main's warning in the previous section, that over-smoothed games feel flat, is the reason to choose deliberately.

### Change the distribution

- **Shuffled decks.** Draw outcomes from a shuffled deck instead of rolling independent chances. A 1-in-10 event becomes one card in a 10-card deck: no repeats, and never more than 10 tries, provided you stop the last card of one shuffle from becoming the first card of the next. You can store a deck as counts per card (which doubles as weighting) to reduce what you track, and either reshuffle when it empties or reset it in the same order ([Evan Debenham 2022, 6:04](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=364)).
- **Pyramid, bell and half-pyramid curves.** Replace a uniform roll with the average of two rolls (pyramid) or three (bell). Debenham's half-pyramid is two thirds of one uniform roll plus one third of another: uniform in the middle, pyramid at the edges. All three make the average more likely and the minimum and maximum less likely, which raises perceived consistency and makes results feel fairer and easier to plan around ([Evan Debenham 2022, 4:03](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=243)).
- **Narrow ranges.** Andrew Aversa kept Tangledeep's damage ranges tight rather than using D20 or D6-style rolls, and replaced item identification with Diablo-style visible random affixes, as part of making actions, skills and items clear ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 7:04](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=424)). Michael Brough applies the same idea to effects: narrow a random effect's range (teleport within the current room, say) and the player gets more information for a wiser choice, even if some good outcomes are excluded ([Michael Brough 2021, 26:56](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=1616)).

### Remember past results

- **Forced averaging.** Adjust an event's chance algorithmically based on past results. Path of Exile does this for evasion so that evasion builds are as reliable as tanking builds; it is common in competitive games, where luck should not decide too much ([Evan Debenham 2022, 9:09](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=549)).
- **Pity timers.** Guarantee a good outcome after enough failures. Debenham notes the mechanism is used manipulatively in loot boxes but can spare a player from grinding forever for a drop ([Evan Debenham 2022, 9:27](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=567)). Ben Berman describes it as making the gambler's fallacy true inside the game (fail 40 times and the system "feels pity" and gives you something awesome anyway), and warns it can be highly addictive for people with gambling problems ([Ben Berman 2017, 33:30](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=2010)).
- **Rubber bands.** Brian Walker generates Brogue's reward rooms, where you may take exactly one of several items, on a rubber band: the probability rises every time a reward room is not generated and drops when one is, so their pace is roughly constant across games and players can assemble a competent character ([Brian Walker 2018, 14:00](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=840)).
- **A loot director.** Benard's loot director for Dead Cells, modelled on the Left 4 Dead director, spots streaks of bad luck: after trash loot four times in a row, it makes sure the fifth drop is something nice ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 27:21](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1641)). Legendary drops are biased toward the player's build (playing bows raises the chance of a legendary bow), and a planned legendary that the player misses, skips or does not buy is placed on their path again later in the run, possibly dropped by an enemy instead of the planned chest ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 28:20](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1700)).

### Budget from the top down

Benard's most transferable idea is to start from a perfectly balanced, non-random allocation, as if the game were not randomised, and then add chaos back under control ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 28:59](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1739)). Gold in Dead Cells is budgeted per level: about 80% of the price of the priciest item, adjusted for the gold the player is carrying and then randomised, so the player can buy something in that level. The budget is then spread deliberately unevenly among chests, enemies and walls, because big piles feel better. Of five enemies, four drop nothing and one drops a big pile: the same total, but a different feeling ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 30:43](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1843)).
