From time to time the game decides in advance that a run will be a lucky "golden run"; the player has no control over it, so it still feels random though it is deliberate ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 28:59](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1739)).

Tyler Coleman reaches a similar place. To make good moments arrive at the intended intervals, you can replace randomness with a hidden fixed cycle that feels random, as Clash Royale's chest cycle does. Coleman's own games borrowed it, with the caution that the approach can verge on dark patterns if misused ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 28:40](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1720)). Max Kreminski's Star Freighter tips the scales on sequence rather than frequency: a passenger hijacking the ship never happens among the player's first three passengers, because as the first event it would seem random and unexceptional, while after a run of safe passengers it lands ([Max Kreminski 2017, 11:14](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=674)).

### Give the player a hand on the roll

Brough argues that random effects are neither intrinsically good nor bad: they regress the situation toward the average. That makes them worth using when things are worse than average, which is why Rogue's scroll of teleport mostly ends up good once identified, since the player chooses when to read it. It also depends on the map: Rogue's large 80x20 levels with few enemies make a random teleport usually safe, while a crowded level would make it risky ([Michael Brough 2021, 21:55](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=1315)). Brough offers two ways to soften a random effect without removing it. First, generate several outcomes and let the player pick: Brough's blink dagger offers two destinations, then three, then four, like drawing two cards and discarding one or rolling two dice and keeping the higher. This keeps some risk, where NetHack's ring of teleport control removes the randomness entirely ([Michael Brough 2021, 26:07](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=1567)). Second, give the player a chance to respond before a bad outcome hurts them, such as an extra turn after teleporting, which avoids Rogue's case of landing in a room of monsters and dying at once ([Michael Brough 2021, 26:56](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=1616)).

> Any random effect can be made a little bit more controlled by having this idea of do it multiple times and pick one. — [Michael Brough 2021, 26:07](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=1567)

Dan DiIorio adopted a rule across Luck be a Landlord: content with a small random chance to trigger should still give a small benefit when it does not trigger, and long-shot chances can be replaced with guaranteed timers. After a playtest, the Coal symbol was reworked to transform after 20 spins rather than on a random chance ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 13:52](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=832)).

### Restrict what gets shuffled

Randomizers, the mods that shuffle an existing game's items or locations, show the same principle at the scale of a whole game. Stella Mazeika says that for complex games players tend to dial wild randomization back; Mazeika imagines a Morrowind randomizer that relocates only key items, giving players guarantees about where they need to go ([Stella Mazeika 2019, 16:02](https://youtu.be/C7laugXEc9s?t=962)).

### Warning cases and odd sources

Smoothing only works if the player cannot route around it. Max Hawkins, who lets a randomizer app choose places to go, insists on accepting the first result whenever it is practical; allow rerolls and you fall into pressing again and again until you get what you already wanted ([Max Hawkins 2019, 15:17](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=917)). The same is true of any reroll, save-scum or "new screen" button you give the player: it turns your randomness into a search.

Coleman also suggests a non-random source of variation. Map the first ten years of a company's stock price onto an item's spawn weight and set the merchant's buy price to its inverse, and items become more common and cheaper over time while players feel they are moving the market: a player who keeps selling apples feels they crashed the price, though it was pre-planned. Coleman uses the first decade after a company lists because it has more rises and falls ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:24:14](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=19454)). Early stock histories suit progression because, like progression, the number usually goes up, but with a real-world chaos that RNG or Perlin noise does not provide. The catch is that the chaos will not always fit (apples becoming abundant just as the player reaches the desert), so you may still need your own modifiers ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:44:18](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=20658)).

### Which tool for which problem

- Miss streaks or droughts of a specific event: a shuffled deck, forced averaging, or a pity timer.
- Damage that swings too wildly to plan around: a pyramid or bell distribution, or a narrower range.
- Bad-luck streaks in loot: a loot director that watches recent drops.
- Never finding the item a build needs: bias drops toward the build and re-place missed key items later in the run.
- Economy runs that leave the player unable to buy anything: budget per level from the top down, then clump it.
- Important rewards arriving at uneven pace across runs: a rubber-banded probability or a hidden fixed cycle.
- A dramatic event that would feel arbitrary if it came too soon: block it from happening first.
- A random effect that kills unfairly: let the player pick from several rolls, narrow its range, or give them a turn to respond.
- Long-shot effects that feel useless: a consolation benefit on failure, or a guaranteed timer.
- A randomizer too chaotic for a complex game: shuffle only key items.

## Push your luck: risk the player chooses

The previous two sections were about randomness that happens to the player. The other kind is risk the player opts into, and several talks treat it as central to roguelike decision-making.

### Choice as an agonising tradeoff

Sersa Victory gives four reasons choices in games are fun and dramatic: they test the player's weighing of tradeoffs, grant agency, create uncertainty and make the player feel smart ([Sersa Victory 2022, 3:17](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=197)). Drawing on Ian Schreiber and Jeff Warrender, Victory says a well-designed choice should be agonising: you want several things and cannot have them all, and every choice type in the talk is a flavour of tradeoff ([Sersa Victory 2022, 4:18](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=258)). The classic roguelike gambles fit that pattern. Using an unidentified item means weighing its danger against how dire things are (surrounded, is reading an unknown scroll in the hope of teleport worth the risk that it is something worse?); out-of-depth monsters threaten but give experience and loot; vaults pair dangerous monsters with powerful treasure ([Sersa Victory 2022, 14:44](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=884)). Tarn Adams uses the same comparison for Dwarf Fortress's villain investigations: making an accusation is like reading an unknown scroll, and false accusations or attacking the wrong bandit camp bring trouble on the player, so the game rewards balancing how much to investigate, and with which tools, against the risk ([Tarn Adams 2018, 21:55](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1315)).

### How push-your-luck games store uncertainty

Nic Tringali's talk on push-your-luck games gives a vocabulary for designing these gambles. Many games feel push-your-luck-ish without feeling alike (Netrunner and Blood Bowl both have the trait), because games give players access to uncertainty in different ways and players interpret it differently ([Nic Tringali 2026, 4:46:33](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17193)). Tringali first framed these three examples as player against world, self and others, then decided that the fundamental difference is how each game stores, transforms and reveals information, which lines up with the three basic sources of randomness: decks, dice and people ([Nic Tringali 2026, 4:54:45](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17685)).

- **Deck: Blackjack.** The push-your-luck lies less in a single hit-or-stand than in playing many rounds against a fixed, already-shuffled shoe. Every card dealt to anyone shifts the odds, so the player watches the whole table and when the shoe is reshuffled, and profits when the numbers run their way over time ([Nic Tringali 2026, 4:48:03](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17283)).
- **Dice: Can't Stop.** In Sid Sackson's game, each round is self-contained and every roll independent. You roll four dice, pair them into sums that advance tracks numbered 2 to 12, and either bank progress or keep rolling, losing the round's progress if you cannot match your chosen sums. The world fades away and the contest is with your own hubris ([Nic Tringali 2026, 4:51:03](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17463)).
- **People: Skull.** Each player has three flowers and a skull, stacks cards face down and wagers how many they can flip without hitting a skull, flipping their own stack first. A player holding a skull must pretend to compete without ever winning the wager, and the others read whether each wager is genuine. You are playing against a person, not a deck or a die ([Nic Tringali 2026, 4:53:59](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17639)).

For a roguelike, the question is which of these your risk resembles, since the difference lies in how information is stored and revealed ([Nic Tringali 2026, 4:54:45](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17685)). By analogy, a dungeon whose contents are fixed at generation and revealed as you explore behaves like a Blackjack shoe; an independent combat roll is closer to Can't Stop; an opponent who might be bluffing is Skull.

### Techniques for risk the player can live with

Busting for nothing is punishing, and the most concrete mitigations come from Jon Perry's Party House in UFO 50. The game runs 25 days, so randomness evens out (a bust in a seven-day game would cost a seventh of your turns); the starting troublemakers still give two popularity, so a bad draw pays something; and busting lets you temporarily ban a guest, which makes consecutive busts less likely ([Jon Perry 2025, 26:32](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1592)). Each of those is a general lever: lengthen the horizon over which luck averages, pay a consolation prize, and make the next failure less likely after one has happened.

Tringali's own The Banished Vault shows risk turning into planning. Hazards are dice rolls on travel or construction that cost an unknown extra resource, such as faith, actions or materials ([Nic Tringali 2023, 4:15](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=255)). Because players know the cost is coming but not how big, the risk becomes a meta-resource: they bring spare materials or an extra exile in case a bad roll costs a navigator their faith ([Nic Tringali 2023, 19:38](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1178)).

Cezar Capacle points to Apocalypse World's three resolution bands: a miss means something unwanted happens, 10+ is full success, and 7 to 9 is success with a cost, compromise or complication. Capacle calls the middle band the Goldilocks zone where players land most often, and the "Indiana Jones effect": resolving one conflict creates the next, so the rolls keep the story moving ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 15:45](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=945)). A partial-success band makes a failed gamble change the run rather than end it.

Limiting a resource per level turns recovery into a gamble. Victory's favourite now-versus-later example is Forays into Norrendrin, which allows one rest per dungeon level, in contrast to roguelikes where you can recover by resting in any corner; the player has to judge how serious the current situation is ([Sersa Victory 2022, 17:01](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1021)). Todd Furmanski's Dragon's Descent offers one pick per level from a treasure room (health, firepower or points), which supports tank, glass-cannon and score-chasing styles; since treasure is often how you heal, low health pushes you to the next level ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 1:56](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=116)).

Some designs make the whole run a push-your-luck structure. The Delve Bros built Stream Heist around money: stealing art earns cash, each day and each capture costs it, and a captured thief loses some cash rather than restarting, so the run ends only when the money runs out ([The Delve Bros 2020, 8:15](https://youtu.be/4jNMv79Xb6A?t=495)). An earlier prototype of the same game framed it as covering daily hacking costs with painting income, a risk-reward call about how much to steal before escaping ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:59:02](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=7142)). Dan Norder's account of Hobbit, a variant of the BASIC game Chase, has the player choose how many orcs to face each round, scoring more for more enemies and bonuses for killing all of them but losing points for dying ([Dan Norder 2024, 20:13](https://youtu.be/ohH6LBM2EiU?t=1213)).

Players invent these structures too. In a Nuzlocke run of Pokémon, already-caught species are rerolled, so Stella Vermilion describes *encounter routing*: in FireRed, catching the Rattata on Route 1 removes it from the pool and makes a Mankey (good against Brock) much more likely, and catching the birds on Routes 1 and 22 nearly triples the chance of a Nidoran, from 15% to 42%. Vermilion calls it one of the coolest places where players work with the RNG ([Stella Vermilion 2026, 8:54:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32062)). Knowing how your pools work and acting on it is a skill, and it fits Harris's intuition test from earlier in this chapter.

### In practice

The good gambles in these talks share three properties. They are **visible**: the player knows a risk is being taken and roughly what is at stake, as with Banished Vault's hazards or a vault's guardians ([Nic Tringali 2023, 19:38](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1178); [Sersa Victory 2022, 14:44](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=884)). They are **voluntary**: the player chooses whether to read the scroll, wager, enter or face more orcs ([Dan Norder 2024, 20:13](https://youtu.be/ohH6LBM2EiU?t=1213)). And they are **recoverable**: a failed gamble costs something (a consolation prize, a partial success, a temporary ban, cash but not the run) without necessarily ending the run ([Jon Perry 2025, 26:32](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1592); [Cezar Capacle 2024, 15:45](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=945); [The Delve Bros 2020, 8:15](https://youtu.be/4jNMv79Xb6A?t=495)). When you add a risk, check all three.

## When the optimal play is the boring play

### The infinite-patience test

Feinberg credits Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup with teaching one way of testing every system. Forget what the system is for, and imagine a player with bottomless patience and infinite tolerance for tedium. How would that player use the system to maximise their chance of winning, and does that play look fun? If not, the design has a problem ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 0:28](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=28)).

The reason this matters even for players who never do it is the key part of the argument. A fun death leaves you planning to teleport sooner or find haste next time. An unfun optimal strategy poisons every death instead: you die thinking that you would have won if only you had sat in a corner training fire magic for several hundred turns, or cast detect monsters every other step ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 5:55](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=355)). NetHack's pudding farming is the warning case. Players split puddings with a weak weapon and sacrificed the corpses for divine rewards; when people complained, one player replied that the punishment for pudding farming is pudding farming. Feinberg calls that a great line and a terrible philosophy, because it puts the fun way to play in conflict with the way most likely to win. NetHack 3.6 removed pudding corpses, which more or less solved it ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 7:00](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=420)).

> A situation like pudding farming puts a game at war with itself. — [Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 7:00](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=420)

John Harris makes the same demand in terms of grind: repetitive make-work that only raises numbers without interesting decisions. Designers should eliminate it, as Crawl's developers have worked hard to do; Harris found Dungeons of Dredmor and Rogue Legacy mostly grind ([John Harris 2016, 7:18](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=438)).

### Angband: slow play was never optimal

Angband's history is the strongest evidence here, because the community believed for years that the boring strategy was the winning one. Nick McConnell describes the long-held belief that ultra-conservative play was optimal, with rules such as never going below dungeon level 20 without free action. That made the 100-level game very long, which made players even more afraid of losing a month's character. In the mid-2000s players showed that aggressive diving wins more games per hour: you lose some characters, but you can take five to level 20 in the time one used to reach level 24. Development now assumes players dive, though Angband does not tell anyone how to play and some still play conservatively ([Nick McConnell 2021, 7:13](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=433)).

Erik Osheim and Robert Au explain why diving works. Traditional play spent millions of turns acquiring resistances and stair-scumming (repeatedly regenerating a shallow level, which Angband generates fresh on every visit, to fish for artifacts). It was boring, and it actually made the game harder, because habits learned at shallow depths fail at deep levels where resting can get you killed in a turn ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 19:59](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1199)). The diving strategy popularised by Eddie Grove, going down as fast as possible and fleeing any uncertain fight, makes stealth and avoidance central, finds better items deeper, and keeps players on edge so they make fewer dumb mistakes and build habits that work at dungeon level 90. Long-time players who had never done well started winning ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 21:17](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1277)). Stair scumming is common enough across the genre to have a community name ([Conference hosts 2019, 16:07](https://youtu.be/HaBp4ETtDKI?t=967)).

The Angband team then nerfed the boring risk-free strategies: object detection became fuzzy so levels have to be explored, teleporting everything away became harder, and the Global Invulnerability spell had already been removed for breaking the game ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 22:58](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1378)). Regenerating levels also leave Angband with a "too much junk" problem late on, since by dungeon level 90 almost everything you find is worse than what you have; the team debated whether to stop generating such items or hide them ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 5:49](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=349)). The forced-descent option that came out of this history is a clock, covered in the next section.

### Smaller cases

Generation rules can reward odd sequencing. NetHack generates a level's monsters when the level is first created, scaled to the player's experience level at that time, so visiting a level early makes it easier to return to later; in a speedrun, Adeon deliberately avoids reaching experience level 15 before the castle for this reason ([Adeon 2017, 5:09](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=309)). Limits on rewards can be raced. Don Worth capped Beneath Apple Manor at one treasure per floor because of Apple II constraints, and some players responded by sprinting to each treasure room without fighting, arriving at level five heavily equipped, while others inched through and died. David Craddock presents this as emergent behaviour that players chose ([David Craddock 2016, 6:50](https://youtu.be/Gs9Nb5ZYRY0?t=410)).

Grind is disliked so widely that Leonard Richardson suggests it may be a rich vein for designers to subvert, along with completionism such as collecting 64,000 bananas for an achievement ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 14:06](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=846)). None of the talks cited here reports doing so.

### Finding degenerate strategies in your own game

For each system, run Feinberg's test: what does a player with infinite patience do with it ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 0:28](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=28))? Look in particular for anything that gets better with time and costs nothing to wait for: regeneration ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 12:44](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=764)), respawning or endlessly spawning monsters ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 15:19](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=919)), regenerating levels ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 19:59](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1199)), divine rewards for repeatable acts ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 7:00](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=420)). Ask whether your community's received wisdom about safe play matches what actually wins most games per hour, as Angband's did not ([Nick McConnell 2021, 7:13](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=433)). And check what your players say after deaths: if they blame skipped grind rather than their own decisions, the optimal strategy is already hurting the game ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 5:55](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=355)). Removing an exploit, as NetHack did with pudding corpses, works for single cases. The general answer to "waiting is always optimal" is to make time cost something, which is what clocks do ([Rosalind Miles Chapman 2020, 2:06](https://youtu.be/j9ykOdQRUQk?t=126)).

## Clocks: hunger, timers and pressure to move on

### What a clock is for

The talks agree on the purpose of a hunger clock, and it is not survival simulation. Rosalind Miles Chapman explains that a roguelike protagonist grows stronger the more they explore and fight, so without time pressure the optimal but unfun strategy is to exhaust every resource before moving on. Hunger turns time into a resource, making thoroughness a strategic choice rather than the obvious one ([Rosalind Miles Chapman 2020, 2:06](https://youtu.be/j9ykOdQRUQk?t=126)). Main generalises it: players will optimise themselves out of fun if a boring behaviour is useful, and many games drift toward ever more careful play, so anything that keeps them pressing forward into the satisfying parts is powerful, as NetHack's hunger pushes players on instead of searching every corner ([Shawn Main 2021, 18:42](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1122)). Santiago Zapata lists Rogue's food timer among the devices that kept the pressure on the player to continue the journey ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 12:37](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=757)), and the Rogue team's own account confirms it was a response to an exploit: players rested by weighting the space bar with a shoe while they went to lunch, so starvation was added ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 9:26](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=566)).

> What hunger does is turns time into a resource. — [Rosalind Miles Chapman 2020, 2:06](https://youtu.be/j9ykOdQRUQk?t=126)

Chapman describes the traditional form: the character weakens, loses health and eventually dies unless they eat, and the food they can bank is capped, which interacts with inventory limits (Pixel Dungeon's horn of plenty takes the trinket slot, a trade-off against other trinkets). Hunger also limits powerful but slow and unfun options such as sleeping to recover ([Rosalind Miles Chapman 2020, 3:08](https://youtu.be/j9ykOdQRUQk?t=188)). Resources can double up: in Caves of Qud fresh water is both the currency and something the player must carry and drink ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 19:33](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=1173)), and speedrunners show how a clock bites differently by pace, since digging straight down with a pickaxe saves NetHack speedrunners enormous time while excessive digging is a common way to starve in normal-paced play ([Adeon 2017, 52:29](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=3149)).

### The clock has been loosening

Feinberg traces the history. In Rogue, a simple game with a harsh clock, every turn until starvation counts, and the food clock acts like a time limit with checkpoints. Starving is not fun, so later roguelikes made food lenient and added complications (monsters eating food, spells costing food) that made balance harder. With classes that need very different amounts of resting and moving, no clock could be tight for fast styles without being impossible for slow ones. The result, in Crawl, is food as a vestigial stub that reins in only the most absurdly time-consuming strategies ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 20:11](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=1211)).

Several designers removed or defanged hunger, for different reasons. Tyriq Plummer added starvation to Catacomb Kids because eating corpses only to restore health felt mechanically boring, and it ruined the pace: time pressure punished the thoughtfulness and caution the game was meant to encourage, and needing to kill to eat made pacifist runs impossible. Plummer removed it quickly ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 21:50](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1310)). Thomas Biskup made hunger in Ultimate ADOM weaken but never kill, because dying to a clock is not fun. Asked how else to stop slow optimal play, Biskup suggests stopping treasure generation on a level while spawning monsters that give less and less experience, or allowing natural healing only some time after leaving a level, and says the right mechanism depends on the game's theme ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:56](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1076)). The Caves of Qud developers considered their hunger system weak and planned a replacement so players would starve less often ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 33:33](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=2013)).

Aversa's Tangledeep is the cautionary tale on the other side, and the most instructive sequence in this material. Aversa removed hunger as artificial difficulty, and experienced players found the optimal strategy became "dancing with monsters": staying a few tiles ahead with a ranged weapon until health regenerated. They reported the game was too easy and full of cheesy tactics ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 12:44](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=764)). Removing health regeneration stopped the kiting but brought back deaths by attrition, unavoidable chip damage wearing down players who played well, which was what Tangledeep had set out to eliminate; Aversa says this made things even worse ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 13:28](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=808)). Feinberg names the same trap in general: DoomRL, Sproggiwood and Desktop Dungeons remove HP and MP regeneration over time, which makes loitering worthless, but this creates new farming exploits around whatever does restore resources. In Sproggiwood, kills restore stamina and spider pots spawn weak spiders endlessly, so it is sometimes right to farm them; Crawl's Deep Dwarves, with no HP regeneration and reliance on vampiric effects, could leave weak enemies on an earlier level as a "vampire farm" ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 15:19](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=919)).

The disagreement, then, is between Plummer and Biskup, who see starvation as punishing the careful play or causing the deaths they want to avoid ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 21:50](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1310); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:56](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1076)), and Aversa, whose game collapsed into a degenerate strategy without one ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 12:44](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=764)). What decides it is whether anything else in your game makes waiting costly: Catacomb Kids wanted caution, while Tangledeep had free regeneration and nothing else pushing the player on.

### Substitutes for hunger

The talks offer many clocks that are not food. They group into three kinds.

**Recovery tied to progress.** Tangledeep's eventual answer was a healing flask that drains as you heal and refills as you explore, so lingering on a floor empties it through constant healing while exploring keeps it topped up. It is backed by healing food on a shared cooldown and campfires that fully heal every few floors. Aversa says it mostly worked, though some players still rejected the lack of rest-to-heal ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 14:26](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=866)). Dylan White's Rift Wizard has no hunger, mana or resting: each spell has limited charges (Fireball 18, Flame Gate four) restored only by scarce mana potions dropped at random, which fill the role food plays elsewhere ([Dylan White 2020, 5:44](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=344)). Forays into Norrendrin's one rest per level, from the push-your-luck section, belongs here too.

**Escalation for staying.** Chapman calls Invisible, Inc. the purest form: everything gets harder the longer you stay ([Rosalind Miles Chapman 2020, 5:44](https://youtu.be/j9ykOdQRUQk?t=344)). The haunts planned for Castle Cthulhu escalate for lingering, with jammed doors and collapsing passages; unlike horror games' mostly aesthetic sanity effects, haunts must be able to kill you, mess up your map and spawn dangerous things, or they will not work as time pressure ([Rosalind Miles Chapman 2020, 7:24](https://youtu.be/j9ykOdQRUQk?t=444)). Plummer notes that in real-time games with regenerating health, a hunger clock reduces to plain time pressure, which Spelunky's ghost (appearing after five minutes) and Crystal Catacombs' timer use to stop players clearing every level and to keep an arcade pace; Crystal Catacombs keeps levels straightforward so the timer only bites very slow players ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 20:15](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1215)). Eric Billingsley's Into Ruins makes jumping into holes the only way down and gives the player an orb of gravity that grants a ticking slowfall status; needing to descend before it runs out, and to find more orbs, replaces the hunger meter ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 26:11](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1571)). Angband's forced-descent option sends you deeper on every return to the dungeon, so players can no longer wait on level 98 for perfect gear before fighting Morgoth; by level 97, only two levels remain before Sauron. The team wanted to encourage diving, not mandate it, so it is an option ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 22:02](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1322)).

**Deadlines and journeys.** Some games give the whole run a time limit. Larn replaces food with 300 "mobuls" of 100 turns each to cure the hero's daughter, extendable by scrolls of time warp; John Harris says the limit is not much of a problem at first but may become one as winning raises the difficulty of the next game ([John Harris 2021, 25:25](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=1525)). Jeff Olson's Alphaman used food, fatigue and a day-night sleep cycle, with night shrinking visibility to adjacent squares, partly to remind players of the one-week deadline for defeating the Grinch ([Jeff Olson 2023, 12:46](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=766)). Sword of Fargoal's timed return trip through brand-new levels came from a memory limit: the Commodore PET could not keep the seed, so the dungeon was explained as magically rearranging itself, and carrying the sword out against a timer, through tougher enemies and unexplored maps, added tension ([David Craddock 2016, 6:18](https://youtu.be/Gs9Nb5ZYRY0?t=378)). Against the Storm turned the Queen's Impatience from a fixed timer into a resource that reputation reduces and that has benefits of its own; the developers call it more mechanic than timer and keep it because pressure is part of the game's identity, though publishers and some players still dislike being rushed ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 28:24](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1704)). Recht describes Sunless Sea as long voyages where fuel, food and crew fear must be planned against a known destination, or you run out and at best limp home ([Dan Recht 2017, 17:16](https://youtu.be/FnJxkId-1eE?t=1036)).

### What goes wrong with clocks

Feinberg gives the sharpest warnings. In a game as large as Crawl, strong clocks would push optimal players to turn off auto-explore and travel automation, since automation wastes turns compared with a careful human, and clearing dozens of huge levels by hand is not fun. Crawl therefore keeps its clocks (at least three: food, piety and out-of-depth spawning) weak, and out-of-combat time stays essentially free ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 21:16](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=1276)). A fixed turn limit, say 4,000 turns to win or die, does make out-of-combat time matter, but it creates "good as dead" games, where a new player in particular has lost long ago but the game lacks the dignity to end itself ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 18:13](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=1093)). Hard checkpoints (reach floor N by turn T) could work only in a simpler game with checkpoints close together and play styles that take similar time; widely spaced checkpoints bring back the already-dead problem ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 26:15](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=1575)). Crawl's turn-count scoring creates an implicit clock for high-score chasers, but they are a small minority Feinberg does not think worth designing for, and because the score counts actions rather than game time it produces exploits like swinging a loaf of bread to rest in fewer turns ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 23:47](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=1427)).

John Bond adds a constraint on where a clock may run. A *breath moment* is a quiet space, such as the threshold of a door, where the player can stay indefinitely and choose when to continue; taking that control away, for example with a timer, always feels bad and is usually avoided outside competitive player-versus-player games ([John Bond 2024, 5:19](https://youtu.be/bpGRyzWCWwk?t=319)).

### Choosing a clock

- **What degenerate strategy is it stopping?** Name it: resting to full, farming a respawning enemy, scumming levels, kiting while regenerating. If you cannot name one, you may not need a clock.
- **Does your game want caution?** If careful, slow play is the point, a clock fights the design, as Catacomb Kids found.
- **What happens if you remove regeneration instead?** Expect attrition deaths and new farms around whatever still restores resources.
- **Does it punish automation?** In a large game, a strong clock makes auto-explore a mistake.
- **Can it produce a living-dead run?** Prefer clocks that weaken or escalate over hard limits that let a lost game drag on.
- **Is it tied to progress?** Recovery that refills by exploring, or pressure that escalates the longer you stay on a level, pushes forward without a global deadline.
- **Does it respect quiet moments?** Leave the player spaces where no clock runs.
- **Does it fit the theme?** Biskup's point: the right mechanism depends on what the game is about, whether that is a flask, a gravity orb, an impatient queen or a voyage.

## Pacing a run: difficulty curves, rhythm and the endgame

A run has a shape. Clocks push the player forward ([Shawn Main 2021, 18:42](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1122)); this section is about what they are pushed toward: how difficulty and reward should move across a single run, and how it should end. The four sections after it widen out to power within a run, balancing methods, difficulty settings and the challenges players set themselves.

### Deeper means harder

The genre's default curve is spatial. Everest Pipkin observes that games about descent, from Rogue and Spelunky to Noita, Dwarf Fortress, Hollow Knight, Cave Story and Animal Well, conventionally grow more complex, more difficult and more alien the deeper you go, so the dungeon's strata map to challenge rather than to historical time ([Everest Pipkin 2026, 29:09](https://youtu.be/VwZS0MQSpaU?t=1749)). Linas Gabrielaitis points out how odd this is: in real geology deeper means older and more primitive, and roguelike progression inverts it, much like the great hole in Don DeLillo's Ratner's Star, where the artifacts grow more advanced the further down you dig ([Linas Gabrielaitis 2023, 7:48](https://youtu.be/jvZb9WoIHxo?t=468)). The convention is useful precisely because it is so familiar: the player reads depth as a difficulty gauge without being told.

### Rhythm: troughs, breaths and the rare moment

A rising curve is not enough on its own; it also needs rhythm. Pandamander argues that you cannot keep stacking excitement. The brain recovers after each spike, so a stream of rare drops followed by mythical ones stops feeling special and starts to feel suspicious, which they say mobile games often get wrong; they compare it to Vegas, where everything is lit all the time and it all starts to look the same ([Pandamander 2024, 5:07](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=307)). Their advice is to keep rare moments rare, leave time for anticipation to build, and plan lows and relaxing stretches, because without them the game goes stale ([Pandamander 2024, 6:27](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=387)).

> You want to keep rare moments rare. You want to allow time for building anticipation. That's the fun part. — [Pandamander 2024, 6:27](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=387)

Tyler Coleman reaches for the same idea from the reward side: deliberately concentrate outcomes so that most of the damage comes from a few attacks (crits, armour breaks) and most of the reward from a few sources such as the boss chest or the secret room, the way D&D sets aside natural 1s and 20s as special ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 26:59](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1619)).

John Bond names the trough; the warning against putting a timer on it appeared under clocks. Roguelikes need "breath" moments, where the game stops asking the player to perform but leaves them in full control for as long as they want. Pausing does not count, because players will not pause to rest; you have to give them a reason to stop trying so hard, and small exploration such as collecting loot, finding a shop or fishing serves. Bond argues that doors, the thresholds between spaces, are where breath works best ([John Bond 2024, 3:59](https://youtu.be/bpGRyzWCWwk?t=239)).

Non-roguelikes offer clean models of interleaved reward. Kristen Yu describes how Animal Crossing runs two quest systems side by side: Nook Miles, a stamp card of one, three or five tasks that is used up once complete and pays a large reward, and Nook Miles+, five single easy tasks that refill as soon as they are done and pay small rewards. The large and small rewards interleave into what Yu calls a satisfying pacing experience ([Kristen Yu 2021, 14:24](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=864)).

### Variable rewards and their limits

Randomised reward is one of the oldest pacing tools in the genre. George Moromisato points to NetHack's chests, which might hold nothing or a wand of wishing: variable rewards reinforce repeat play, much as Moromisato's dog pulled harder on the leash once pulling only sometimes worked. The caveat is that this must be part of a complete design rather than the only mechanic, or it becomes a slot machine ([George Moromisato 2016, 21:47](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1307)). Pipkin makes the same point about digging in farming games such as Stardew Valley, where turning up soil for a random object from a pool works like a scratch card, a piece of micro-gambling that can be addictive ([Everest Pipkin 2026, 11:24](https://youtu.be/VwZS0MQSpaU?t=684)). Animal Crossing gates the loop by real time, scattering three fossils at marked spots each day so digging becomes a daily chore with the hope of the one skull you still need ([Everest Pipkin 2026, 13:07](https://youtu.be/VwZS0MQSpaU?t=787)). Pipkin's warning is that mining games commonly wrap this loop in upgrade and automation systems that are often little more than Skinner boxes, where each better shovel moves the player toward engaging with the world ever more automatically ([Everest Pipkin 2026, 15:04](https://youtu.be/VwZS0MQSpaU?t=904)). Two speakers, a decade apart, converge on the same caution: a variable reward is a spice, not a meal.

### Tools for shaping the curve

Once you know the shape you want, the techniques for producing it are often very simple.

- **Raise the ceiling with progress.** Adrian Herbez's 3D-printed roguelike Plarl splits rooms into thirds (empty, helpful, harmful) with effects of 1 to 6 points, and raises the maximum of the random range as the player moves north toward the exit, so early rooms deal one or two damage and rooms near the exit up to six ([Adrian Herbez 2019, 9:52](https://youtu.be/cGvig1f68Tg?t=592)). The randomness stays; only its ceiling moves.
- **Add elements one at a time.** Rich Wilson describes Prey: Mooncrash starting calm and layering in hazards and variation as players progress, so they get used to each element before the end reaches a fever pitch ([Rich Wilson 2021, 19:36](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1176)).
- **Scale along two axes.** Mark Johnson notes that procedural riddle chains scale difficulty easily, because both the complexity of each step and the number of steps can rise without limit; Johnson rates the demo puzzle about 2 to 3 out of 10 and plans harder, multi-faceted chains as the player gets more skilled ([Mark Johnson 2023, 29:04](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1744)).
- **Bracket, then shuffle.** For Netflix's Cat Burglar, Phenry Ewing's team play-tested trivia questions on 5,000 US adults, 25 questions each, and used the measured success rates (about 12% to almost 90% on three-question sets) to sort the questions into six difficulty brackets ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 20:14](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1214)). The game orders brackets by difficulty but randomises within each, so the first playthrough feels punishingly hard and repeat plays feel gradually easier once the learning effect is accounted for; Ewing says that without simulation the sequencing would have been guesswork ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 23:57](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1437)).
- **Let the structure ramp itself.** Gavin Verhey points out that paper Magic's eight-player draft pairs winners with winners, so the last match is between two undefeated players: a natural ramp that resembles a PvE run that begins with a random encounter and ends against the strongest opponent ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 17:35](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1055)).

A strict curve is not the only option. Tim Keenan resisted ordering Duskers' systems strictly from easy to hard. Sometimes a hard system turns up second, which occasionally upset players, but the more that was embraced the better the stories became: surviving with only two drones left is the near-death tale Keenan sees as the genre's brilliance ([Tim Keenan 2017, 13:49](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=829)). The choice is between a curve the player can trust and a curve that occasionally betrays them for the sake of drama; Cat Burglar's brackets and Duskers' looseness are the two ends.

### The final act

The end of a run deserves its own design. NetHack's is the classic case: taking the Amulet of Yendor alerts every monster, and the repeatedly resurrecting Wizard of Yendor harasses the player all the way back up, stealing the Amulet, cursing items and summoning monsters; leaving without noticing the theft simply loses the game ([Adeon 2017, 45:00](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=2700)). Noah Swartz stresses that getting the Amulet is only part of the game, because the escape adds confusion, teleportation and pursuit, and draws a parallel with the flight from the collapsing tombs in Le Guin's The Tombs of Atuan ([Noah Swartz 2021, 7:13](https://youtu.be/IVDN5GDTIvY?t=433)). Not every part of it lands: the commentators on Adeon's speedrun call the mechanic that randomly drags the Amulet-carrier back down levels a really annoying one that forces levels to be replayed, and experienced players pre-dig direct stair-to-stair paths on the way down to blunt it ([Adeon 2017, 1:34:45](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=5685); [Adeon 2017, 45:00](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=2700)).

The return journey has proved durable. Jonathan Lessard reports that testers of Chogue, a chess-and-Rogue hybrid, resisted the game ending the moment the black king was captured, because a player on a good run does not want to stop; the designers adopted Rogue's actual ending instead, capturing the King of Yendor and returning to the surface ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 22:06](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=1326)). Phillip Daigle modelled Rogue's Gate's win condition on the same shape: retrieve items of power from the tops of six towers on a generated world map and bring them back to a shrine ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 4:26](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=266)).

How you state the goal matters as much as its shape. Wilson describes Prey: Mooncrash giving high-level goals, chiefly a checklist of escaping with all five characters in five different ways, and telling players what to do but not how, so the run became a puzzle box, in the spirit of "get to the bottom of the dungeon" ([Rich Wilson 2021, 20:45](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1245)). Endgames can also revalue powers that looked useless: in Nick Bush's Word Processor, tab-based movement seems pointless early, when the player can often warp anywhere, but becomes essential at the end because it is the only way to outrun a double-speed admin horizontally ([Nick Bush 2026, 39:10](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=2350)).

The size of the unit you are pacing is itself a choice. Verhey explains that MTG Arena defaults to best-of-one because most players have more fun facing many varied opponents, like varied roguelike encounters, even though best-of-three rewards skill and allows sideboarding, which competitive players prefer ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 18:57](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1137)).

**In practice:** decide the shape of the curve and the final act before you tune numbers. Sketch where the troughs and breath moments fall ([Pandamander 2024, 6:27](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=387); [John Bond 2024, 3:59](https://youtu.be/bpGRyzWCWwk?t=239)), how the ceiling of danger rises ([Adrian Herbez 2019, 9:52](https://youtu.be/cGvig1f68Tg?t=592)), and what the last stretch asks of the player ([Adeon 2017, 45:00](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=2700); [Rich Wilson 2021, 20:45](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1245)). Then decide whether the curve is strict (brackets) or loose (shuffled), knowing the loose version will sometimes upset players and sometimes produce a great story ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 23:57](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1437); [Tim Keenan 2017, 13:49](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=829)).

## Power within a run: broken combos, power fantasy and variety

### Let the player outgrow the enemy

Single-player roguelikes are not competitive games, and several designers argue they should not be balanced like one. Dan DiIorio of Luck be a Landlord puts it bluntly: in League of Legends or chess, an overpowered piece gives one side an unfair edge, but in a roguelike the other side is everything between the player and the win condition, and enemies do not have feelings. An extra queen ruins chess but not a roguelike ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 6:45](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=405)).

> Your players will have more fun if they become more powerful than their enemies. — [Dan DiIorio 2025, 6:45](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=405)

The run reset is what makes this safe. Courtney Liessen argues that roguelikes suit game-breaking combos because the benefit lasts only until the run ends, and players already see runs as transient; breaking the guardrails for too long leads to boredom, but an overpowered combo simply speeds up a run it then feels natural to end and restart ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 11:46](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=706)). Against the Storm builds that idea into its structure: once every species is happy the run completes in a minute or two, because the designers do not want the player satisfied for too long and control pressure from both sides ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 29:28](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1768)). DiIorio applies it to patching, preferring, like Dota, to buff weak content rather than nerf strong content, since an overbuffed combo in a single-player game can become a fun new story ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 25:18](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=1518)).

Big swings in power are also something players can steer. Alice Lai explains that known combos in Hades let players shape their own power and difficulty curve: take an early combo and breeze through two areas but struggle later, or suffer early and grab the enabler in the last area to leap ahead, which produces a feeling of mastery ([Alice Lai 2021, 5:46](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=346)). Brian Cronin describes Monster Train's deliberately wild power scale, where a basic card deals 2 damage for 1 ember and another deals 100 piercing damage to every unit for 3, compared with the modest Copper-to-Woodcutter step in Dominion; players enjoy it ([Brian Cronin 2021, 3:01](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=181)). Danny Day describes Desktop Dungeons turning nearly everything into a resource, including which enemy levels you fight, item conversion and racial traits, so that by the boss you are throwing the kitchen sink at it ([Danny Day 2018, 1:38](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=98)). Jon Perry takes the idea to the win condition in UFO 50's Mini and Max: victory means accumulating a fungible currency, so every thread the player follows in a fully open game moves them forward ([Jon Perry 2025, 7:54](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=474)).

### The counterweight: no dominant strategy

Power spikes are welcome; a single strategy that always wins is not. Pandamander argues that a strategy that can roll through 100% of the time removes the moments when play breaks into new possibility space, and that this is what separates games that last 50 hours from games that last 5,000 ([Pandamander 2024, 15:21](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=921)). The Against the Storm designers rejected city walls, though they looked fantastic, because a system that impactful would be built every run, making every town look the same and adding a chore ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 10:02](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=602)). Nic Tringali designs The Banished Vault so that the player's search for an optimal route never finds a single clear path: there must always be options, two difficult routes or a tradeoff ([Nic Tringali 2023, 19:17](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1157)). Three independent talks arrive at the same rule: an option every run must take is not an option.

Content volume is the other defence. Casey Yano says a roguelike has to reach a tipping point of content density where it becomes unpredictable even to its developers; if every player always goes for the same build, there is not enough randomisation, and Yano suspects many roguelites enter early access before reaching that point ([Casey Yano 2022, 28:45](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=1725)).

Not everyone thinks dominance can be eliminated. Tyler Coleman argues that about 20% of a game's items, characters or combos will naturally dominate its meta, that spreading the meta across most content is close to utopian, and that you should instead let a discoverable meta exist and keep it shifting with updates, modes and modifiers, because people enjoy figuring it out ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 25:38](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1538)). Hades bounds the problem structurally: Lai describes "bumpers" such as no more than two or three hammers, four gods and two Hermes boons per run, which limit how wide or deep a build gets and reduce, without eliminating, screen-filling chaos ([Alice Lai 2021, 28:20](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1700)). The disagreement is one of ambition: Pandamander and Yano push for enough room that no strategy dominates, Coleman accepts a dominant slice and keeps it moving.

### Variety within a run and between runs

Tim Keenan offers a frame for where variety should come from. It has two dimensions, within a run and between runs, and you should choose deliberately where your game sits on that slider rather than defaulting to one end; neither end is better, and only on a second roguelike did it become a conscious decision ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:33:45](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30825)). Duskers aimed for as much of the possibility space as possible in every run, which gave great variety within a run but meant different runs kept meeting the same things, like running through the same crazy forest from a different angle ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:34:29](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30869)). By Keenan's estimate, Slay the Spire, FTL and Shogun Showdown sit towards between-run variety because their varying starting conditions shape later synergies, while Kingdom and Below put fewer walls between runs and still offer plenty of variety as you play ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:37:53](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31073)).

Whatever the setting, repetition erodes it. Nat Alison describes settling on a favourite deck, learning its strategies and getting bored: the chaos becomes tame, the patterns rote, and the trees all start looking the same ([Nat Alison 2024, 16:29](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=989)). (Alison's remedy, self-imposed challenge, closes this chapter.)

### Forms of in-run progression

How the player grows inside a run is a design choice with consequences for flexibility, theme and balance.

- **Items rather than levels.** Jasper Cole argues that item-based progression is tangible and flexible: permanent level-up choices lock in a build, while an inventory can be reorganised as challenges change. In Backpack Hero all progression comes through items, with seven drops to choose from after each fight ([Jasper Cole 2023, 22:37](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1357)). Levelling still exists, but it opens new backpack spaces, which Cole considers the best-working part of the game because the progression is visible and fits the collecting theme ([Jasper Cole 2023, 23:27](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1407)).
- **Information as progression.** Jongwoo Kim found that spatial expansion and tech upgrades clashed with The Shrouded Isle's isolated, declining island, so progression comes through information instead: inquiring once reveals a rumour about a villager's hidden trait, twice reveals its full effect. The villagers never change; only the player's perception does ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 17:31](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1051)). Investigation pays off mechanically: fully revealing that a villager is a major sinner before sacrificing them softens their house's anger and restores the related virtue ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 19:23](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1163)). Tarn Adams describes the same pattern in Dwarf Fortress's villain investigations, where each solved link points to the next and villains reacting to your presence supply both danger and clues, forming a game spiral that rises into new mechanisms ([Tarn Adams 2018, 25:41](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1541)).
- **Scarce, fixed budgets.** Rift Wizard has exactly 25 levels with three skill points each and no way to grind, so every purchase must be made carefully ([Dylan White 2020, 4:25](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=265)).
- **Wishes and kits.** In NetHack, wishes let players fill gaps in an "ascension kit" of near-essential items, and an early wish greatly raises the chance of winning; in Adeon's run, an early wish produced blessed, fixed +2 silver dragon scale mail for reflection, keeping the amulet slot free for life saving ([Adeon 2017, 14:53](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=893)).
- **Growth on both sides.** Lessard found Chogue had an asymmetry: as in chess the player only lost pieces, while as in Rogue the enemies grew stronger. The fix borrowed Rogue items that grant new party members, treating party size as the equivalent of hit points, capped at 16 to match chess's 16 pieces ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 21:02](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=1262)).

### Rarity, sets and forced failure as balance tools

Rarity lets you place power. Cole calls it the simplest of Backpack Hero's balance systems: common items should be weaker and broader and fine to find several times, while legendary items can be stronger and more complex because players rarely see more than one or two per run ([Jasper Cole 2023, 18:45](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1125)). Alexander King shows a different lever: sets solve the problem of getting bad cards into a deck voluntarily. In Card Hunter a player accepts an item that mixes strong and harmful cards and plans to mitigate the downside, where Monster Train's events force bad cards in ([Alexander King 2025, 18:35](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=1115)). And when players control generation, they will sometimes build weak characters: Gabriel Koenig's Test Tube Titans forces players to create new titans, so they see more variety and learn which traits are desirable; Koenig calls encouraging failure the essential condition for handing players the reins of generation ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 11:47](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=707)).

**In practice:** let power spike inside a run, especially when the player has chosen it ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 6:45](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=405); [Alice Lai 2021, 5:46](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=346)), and let the run end soon after the player has clearly won ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 29:28](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1768); [Courtney Liessen 2024, 11:46](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=706)). Cap breadth rather than peaks, as Hades' bumpers do ([Alice Lai 2021, 28:20](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1700)), keep rare power rare ([Jasper Cole 2023, 18:45](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1125)), and watch for any option so strong that every run takes it ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 10:02](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=602); [Pandamander 2024, 15:21](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=921)). Decide where your variety lives, within runs or between them, before you build content for the wrong end ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:33:45](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30825)).

## Balancing with data, simulation and play

### Decide what balanced means first

Balance is not a single target. Phenry Ewing argues that before you simulate anything you must decide the desired player experience, because it differs by game: even odds for Werewolf, hard but quickly rewarding for Cat Burglar, and for Neo Cab a constant near-precarity in which players always feel about to run out of money or fuel or get fired but almost never actually run aground ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 29:00](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1740)). Kim's Shrouded Isle is a case of balancing to a mindset: with no reference games to borrow tuning from, Kim kept trades at about even or slightly worse to match the intended paradigm of sustained or slow decline, mostly by trial and error with some help from beta analytics ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 26:45](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1605)).

> First decide what you are designing for and Monte Carlo can help you achieve that before you launch real players. — [Phenry Ewing 2022, 29:00](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1740)

### Three converging methods

The talks describe three methods (play, models and data) and, tellingly, the people who use them most use them together.

**Feel, spreadsheets and simulation.** Jon Perry balances games such as UFO 50's Party House with a three-pronged approach: heavy playtesting by feel (would I still always buy this guest if it cost one more?), spreadsheet valuation of resources like money and popularity, and Monte Carlo simulation, each reinforcing the others. Perry warns you can get lost in the maths, which only gets you close; balancing is not an exact science ([Jon Perry 2025, 19:45](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1185)). Bots establish a no-strategy baseline: one buys nothing and only saves for star guests, using a simple expected-value rule for when to end the party. If such a strategy can win, the design is broken, because the intent is for people to buy things ([Jon Perry 2025, 21:34](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1294)). The same reasoning produced Party House's odd popularity cap of 65, derived from star-guest costs so players cannot hoard until they can buy all four winning guests at once; designers avoid such unround numbers, but sometimes the right number is odd ([Jon Perry 2025, 23:08](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1388)).

**Monte Carlo simulation.** Ewing's simulations of Werewolf showed surprising effects every time a variable changed, such as adding a seer raising the villagers' chance of winning by roughly 25 to 30 percent in some scenarios, even though the model ignored skill and human slips ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 14:54](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=894)). Neo Cab's economy of driver rating, emotional state and money for fuel could produce an unrecoverable game over, out of fuel and money at once, which the team needed to prevent without knowing how ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 26:11](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1571)). Simulation gave them the confidence to tune variables they would otherwise have been too scared to touch, such as fuel cost, starting money, fuel per mile and firing rules ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 27:50](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1670)). Jurie Horneman used simulated random player paths through generated levels to get probability distributions of rooms seen and enemies met for progression balancing ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 24:49](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1489)). Lachlan Kingsford goes further with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS, an AI that plays out many random continuations of a game to choose a move): the whole search tree, not just its chosen move, is a rich sample of feasible game states that can be mined for heat maps and winning-move statistics. In Emu Bay Railway Company it revealed that the important Hobart-Launceston rail link was never built, a problem humans would take a long time to spot; Kingsford had mixed success feeding 10,000 terminal states into the Optuna optimisation framework to tune constants ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 24:26](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1466)).

**Data from real players.** Alan Malloy describes Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup checking complaints against death statistics and replays. When players called the new iron giants oppressive, the developers compared death rates across the Hell branches, found Dis the deadliest with iron giants among its top killers, and watched replays to judge whether those deaths were fun; dying is fine, Malloy says, as long as players have fun and feel they deserved it ([Alan Malloy 2017, 19:54](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1194)). Tournament data even caught a bug: the 0.16 tournament win rate came in at almost twice 0.15's 1.5 percent, someone noticed within a week, and the fix was a commit to stop doubling all player damage ([Alan Malloy 2017, 18:24](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1104)). Evan Debenham uses anonymous analytics in Shattered Pixel Dungeon, comparing how often players invest upgrades in a new item with others in its class and how often those runs win, as a somewhat objective measure of power ([Evan Debenham 2021, 9:54](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=594)). Cole argues that a game with 865 items, like Backpack Hero, cannot be balanced through conversations with players alone and needs run analytics on character, items taken and skipped, killers and outcomes ([Jasper Cole 2023, 21:41](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1301)). The Against the Storm designers track perks and buildings chosen, basic actions and events, to keep a balanced background against which their spiky, interesting perks can stand out ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 15:51](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=951)).

### Where the numbers lie

Every source of balance data has a bias, and the speakers are candid about them.

- **Survivorship.** Benjamin Berman warns that analytics for permadeath games skew toward skilled players, because people who lose just stop playing and never show up in your data; your community may be two standard deviations above a random person ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 16:55](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1015)).
- **Correlation.** Debenham notes that Shattered's top-tier weapons show very high win rates mainly because players only invest in them late in runs they are already winning, and that numerically viable mechanics are not necessarily fun, which is why player feedback is the second source Debenham relies on ([Evan Debenham 2021, 10:13](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=613)).
- **Invisible power.** A big mismatch between analytics and sentiment always has a reason. An item with very low usage but a very high win rate often has passive power, such as faster health regeneration, that players do not notice but that strongly affects winning ([Evan Debenham 2021, 27:51](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1671)).
- **Unwatched systems.** Patrick Kemp describes a community spreadsheet in Cozy Grove exposing an uncommon chair that players crafted repeatedly for profit; Spry Fox had missed it because prices fell out of procedural mods and variants and nobody set them by hand ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 22:35](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1355)). Malloy contrasts the quickly caught damage bug with an exploit that went unnoticed in Crawl since version 0.8 because no milestone tracked it ([Alan Malloy 2017, 18:24](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1104)).
- **Public reaction.** Cole reports that Backpack Hero drew criticism for being too public about analytics: some players disliked items being made worse because the data showed they were too good ([Jasper Cole 2023, 21:41](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1301)).
- **Speed of discovery.** Verhey warns that with fast data sharing, any flaw in a format is found and exploited within a day or two, so Magic includes answers at common rarity for anything that might prove too strong ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 29:07](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1747)).

### Structural levers

Some balance comes from structure rather than numbers.

- **Self-balancing pools.** Verhey describes draft as a fail-safe for a game that cannot be patched: if one colour is overpowered, more players fight over it and get weaker decks, while the lone drafter of a weak colour gets all of it ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 10:09](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=609)).
- **Size.** In a spatial inventory, Cole notes, smaller items are generally more effective and easier to fit, so growing a machete from three spaces to four or shrinking it to two changes its power as surely as its damage number ([Jasper Cole 2023, 19:44](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1184)).
- **Sets.** King argues that balancing sets of cards gives more levers than balancing single cards: you can weaken the good card, soften the bad one, or change the set's composition ([Alexander King 2025, 12:58](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=778)).
- **Singleton pools.** Singleton drafting forces every card to be balanced against all others within its tier, demands a large pool of viable cards, and needs pruning to remove bad ones ([Alexander King 2025, 5:39](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=339)).
- **A counter-resource.** Eric Billingsley ties stealth to light in Into Ruins, so if stealth proves too strong you add light sources such as torch-carrying enemies or staves that illuminate the caster ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 24:12](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1452)).

Economies need their own care. Kim keeps The Shrouded Isle in "volatile stagnation": the overall size of the economy stays roughly constant while individual resources swing widely, producing cascading crises without spiralling up or down; one advisor choice can raise ignorance and fervour, lower obedience and set a rival house plotting ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 9:40](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=580)). Robin Mendoza cautions that organically fluctuating prices can be volatile, chaotic and exploitable, so you may prefer setting prices by fiat to protect balance ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 8:51](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=531)). Jeff Lait describes the "wall", a resource that seems free and constant until it suddenly runs out: in Warlords, Lait's whole army vanished on the turn the gold hit zero, after a war chest had long masked upkeep exceeding income. A modern design would warn the player; Lait leaves open whether games should ([Jeff Lait 2025, 11:48](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=708)).

### Small turns of the dial

The last lesson is that small changes go a long way, and that some teams end up tuning by hand. DiIorio's "big buffs update" for Luck be a Landlord made minuscule changes, such as raising the Watering Can bonus from 10 to 12 coins, because players are often one coin short of winning; a seemingly inconsequential increase turned many losses into wins without alienating players who wanted a challenge ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 15:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=910)). Tringali describes The Banished Vault abandoning numbers derived from simulated planet physics in favour of hand-tuned values found through heavy testing, and late in development starting players on the easiest of three difficulties after the team had always played on the middle one, and adds that the team found the game hard and mentally taxing to play themselves ([Nic Tringali 2023, 28:32](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1712)).

**In practice, a balancing loop:**

1. Write down the experience you want: even odds, hard-but-rewarding, near-precarity ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 29:00](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1740)).
2. Value resources in a spreadsheet and simulate, including a dumb no-strategy bot that must not be able to win ([Jon Perry 2025, 19:45](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1185); [Jon Perry 2025, 21:34](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1294)).
3. Play it by feel and tune by hand ([Nic Tringali 2023, 28:32](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1712)).
4. Ship analytics, but read them against their biases: survivors, late-run selection, invisible power ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 16:55](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1015); [Evan Debenham 2021, 10:13](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=613); [Evan Debenham 2021, 27:51](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=1671)).
5. Check complaints against deaths and replays before acting ([Alan Malloy 2017, 19:54](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1194)), and prefer small buffs to public nerfs ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 15:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=910); [Jasper Cole 2023, 21:41](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1301)).

## Difficulty settings and who they serve

### Hand the dial to the player

There is no single right difficulty, and the designers who have tried hardest to find one say so. Andrea Roberts argues that difficulty is subjective and balance is never perfect: some players want to relax, others want intense challenge, and capabilities differ, so the designer's job is to give players tools to tune the game themselves. In Roundguard those tools include class choice, scoring and stackable relics ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 18:16](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1096)). Philomena Schwab adds that different players find different parts of a game hard. In Niche some players wanted animals to live three times longer so they could pass on genes, while others wanted to pick their starting genetics because some starting genes made certain biomes unwinnable; granular settings for lifespan, damage, starting genetics, food, predators and hidden genes serve more players than a single slider ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 7:34](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=454)).

Andrew Aversa reached the same place with Tangledeep. After players kept rejecting the lack of health regeneration (the flask story told under clocks), Aversa added individual toggles, such as regeneration in hardcore mode or making every monster a champion, tucked into character creation, mixable with any mode, and framed as not the intended way to play, like cheat codes or wizard mode. They are, by this account, universally liked and also enrich the daily and weekly challenges ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 26:46](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1606)).

> When you can't figure it out in the difficulty, just let the players do it. — [Andrew Aversa 2018, 26:46](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1606)

The commercial case points the same way. Dylan Gedig reports that Peglin's easy and hard modes, and later its Cruciball levels, greatly widened its reach among streamers, who play at every skill level ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 25:33](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1533)). DiIorio's experience with Luck be a Landlord shows why a base-difficulty change cannot settle the question: in early access the game was made harder in response to "too easy" complaints, which only produced "too hard" complaints; adding 20 selectable, unlockable difficulty levels, like Slay the Spire's Ascension, stopped both ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 2:29](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=149)).

### Adapting difficulty without a menu

Several games tune difficulty through structure rather than settings.

- **Scripted, then random.** Schwab describes The Wandering Village's easier modes front-loading a scripted sequence before handing over to the same fully random game veterans play: fully scripted for about two hours, partially random until hour five, then fully random, with a shorter partially scripted start in adept mode. It took about a week using existing tools; difficulty complaints dropped and more reviews now call the game too easy, freeing the team to build a harder mode ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 10:40](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=640)).
- **Complications unlocked by mastery.** Roberts describes Roundguard holding back complications and pushing them into the generator as players prove they understand the game: reaching halfway through an act unlocks a new board element that then appears everywhere, beating the act 2 boss unlocks chaos rooms that change map generation, and beating the game unlocks rule-changing relics. Because players repeat the early floors most, this keeps them fresh for veterans without overwhelming newcomers, and Roberts frames it as giving players more ways to express what they have learned ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 12:35](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=755)).
- **A choice of director.** Schwab singles out RimWorld's storytellers, which let players choose between difficulty that adapts to what they are doing and a completely random experience, answering complaints that games feel too random or too scripted ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 12:28](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=748)).
- **Difficulty as geography.** Niche lets players pick difficulty by direction of travel from each generated island: left is easier, right keeps it the same, up is harder; struggling players can retreat or stay and stockpile food before moving on ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 6:13](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=373)). Zeno Rogue's HyperRogue scales difficulty per land: collecting treasure makes that land harder, but moving to another land resets to easy, and high scores unlock content ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 20:58](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1258)).
- **Optional side dungeons.** Tangledeep's Dreamcaster, borrowed from Disgaea's item worlds, lets players enter any piece of equipment as a mini-dungeon, picking an encounter difficulty and powering up gear. Aversa added it after analytics showed a sharp drop-off after the first boss, as a limited form of grinding for an otherwise linear 20-floor crawl ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 23:15](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1395)).
- **Information as the dial.** In Bjarke Alexander Larsen's Discord logic puzzle, the number of facts revealed up front sets difficulty (four of five needed facts is easy, two is hard), and the game shows how corrupted an entry is so players choose ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 12:25](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=745)).
- **Layered content.** Jamie Brittain points to Spelunky's Eggplant run and multiple endings: roguelikes create large amounts of content that not every player will see, so hardcore players get a whole extra game while others are free to stop early ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 23:48](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1428)).

### What goes wrong

Options can mislead, fail to motivate or alienate. Roberts' mercy relic in Roundguard gave frustrated players training wheels and was worded so nobody felt talked down to, but streamers equipped it for its extra potions and stats without realising it was easy mode, risking a wrong impression of the game; an update added the words "easy mode" up front ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 23:25](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1405)). Label easy modes respectfully and clearly; the two are not in conflict. Lisa Brown notes that difficulty tiers which give no benefit do not motivate players whose taste for challenge serves concrete goals: Brown played Slay the Spire's Ascension 1 only because it adds elites and so relics, and feels no loss in skipping Ascension 20 ([Lisa Brown 2020, 14:42](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=882)). Mike Cook observes that generated rule variants can alienate players whose expectations come from the main game: many skip a Slay the Spire daily challenge when they see an unwelcome modifier, such as one removing map decisions, because the mode is not communicated well ([Mike Cook 2023, 12:14](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=734)).

**In practice:** pick a default that lets newcomers through, as The Banished Vault eventually did by starting players on easy ([Nic Tringali 2023, 28:32](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1712)), and put challenge on top as unlockable tiers rather than raising the floor ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 2:29](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=149)). Prefer specific toggles to a single slider, present them as optional, and say plainly what each does. Where you can, let the world carry difficulty (routes, lands, unlocks) so players choose it by playing rather than through a menu. If a harder tier gives nothing, expect only challenge-seekers to take it.

## Self-imposed challenge: conducts, bonus objectives and alternate rules

Some players, having beaten your game or grown tired of it, make it harder on purpose. You can ignore them, or you can learn from them and support them.

### What conduct play is and what it tells you

Kawa defines conduct play as deliberately changing a game's rules from those initially stated, usually to make it harder, either as challenges players invent or as ones the game tracks; the tracked kind is now mostly known as achievements, though other forms exist ([Kawa 2019, 3:33](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=213)). Kawa's advice to developers is to treat it as a diagnostic: ask which mechanics in your game are easy or hard to ignore, what it implies when high-level players alter them, and what skills your game is really asking for ([Kawa 2019, 20:08](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=1208)). Finding it inspiring that any game's mechanics can be pulled apart to create new challenges, Kawa suggests designers embrace that ([Kawa 2019, 15:48](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=948)).

> There is so much room within any given play space for people to examine their mechanics, pull them apart and create challenges from them. — [Kawa 2019, 15:48](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=948)

Not every conduct is about difficulty. Kawa notes that players are also motivated by role-play and by removing tedium, as with NetHack's polypile-less conduct, which drops an awful but unnecessary mechanic, and that some conducts make the game easier by narrowing the decision tree, such as sticking to one weapon or never switching gods in Crawl ([Kawa 2019, 24:50](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=1490)).
