Nat Alison sees challenge runs, speedrunning and mods as the way players restore a game whose balance has gone stale, amending the existing content to find something new, just as mathematicians find interest among large numbers through special classes like Mersenne primes ([Nat Alison 2024, 17:23](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=1043)).

### Games that track the challenge

NetHack is the reference case. It tracks voluntary conducts such as vegan, pacifist, wishless and illiterate play and reports them at game end, effectively optional challenge modes ([Adeon 2017, 1:21:44](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=4904)). Drew Streib explains why this matters for serial winners: high score tracks improvement only until a player ascends (wins), after which low-turn, low-score and high-conduct ascensions are the more impressive feats, because a better player does not need to stockpile preparation; Streib would like more statistics on conducts ([Drew Streib 2016, 19:29](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1169)).

ADOM shows a community building challenges around a single place. Its small cave spawns a stronger monster every time you kill one, a design meant to teach that you need not fight to get what you need ([Kawa 2019, 5:28](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=328)). The Eternium Man challenge turns that on its head, asking players to reach maximum level solely inside the cave: very hard, technically faster than the main game, and a pure test of combat knowledge ([Kawa 2019, 6:56](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=416)). ADOM players have gone to extremes, winning with only a drakeling's breath weapon or under a 100-stone carry limit when a single chaos orb weighs 100 ([Kawa 2019, 23:21](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=1401)). Hoplite formalises the same move: its altar gifts feel essential but are technically optional, so it tracks runs that never use altars and also offers a daily challenge of three very hard levels with an arbitrary skill set ([Kawa 2019, 15:00](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=900)).

### Building alternate rules into the game

Designers can ship the rule changes themselves. John Harris describes Shiren 5's 20 to 30 bonus dungeons with distinct twists, one like Minesweeper, one like Sokoban with monsters, one where you never level past 1 and flee monsters throughout, giving dozens of hours of replay value ([John Harris 2024, 25:15](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=1515)). Tom Francis's Heat Signature attaches clauses such as no kills, no witnesses or ghost to its high-paying missions; under ghost, being seen is failure, so even the least armoured guard becomes as dangerous as the nastiest boss ([Tom Francis 2023, 12:25](https://youtu.be/3vSCncV5hkI?t=745)).

Optional objectives inside a fight serve players of every skill at once. Roberts describes Roundguard's roaming scarab, which moves between pegs and multiplies the points of everything hit after it; chasing it, sometimes instead of grabbing needed health, is a press-your-luck choice that raises difficulty for score-focused players without changing any system ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 20:52](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1252)). Shawn Main makes the same point with a golden wisp worth extra gold: a novice is happy to win the battle, a medium player to take no damage, and a skilled player can also chase the wisp ([Shawn Main 2021, 17:01](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1021)).

Younès Rabii offers a frame for a game's modes as states of matter. Slay the Spire's hand-tuned standard mode is solid, its Daily Challenge with random character and modifiers is gaseous and less pruned, and Custom mode, where players toggle modifiers themselves, is liquid: the most complex, and configurable into either of the others ([Younès Rabii 2025, 26:02](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1562)). The custom mode is where player-invented challenges and designer-shipped ones meet.

**In practice:** watch what your best players choose to ignore; it tells you which mechanics are optional and which are load-bearing ([Kawa 2019, 20:08](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=1208)). Track conducts and turn counts and show them at game end, so serial winners have something to chase ([Adeon 2017, 1:21:44](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=4904); [Drew Streib 2016, 19:29](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1169)). Offer optional in-fight objectives and rule-twist modes that layer challenge without touching the base game, and consider a custom mode that lets players assemble their own.

## Tensions and open questions

**Remove unfair deaths, or expect them?** Most teams in this chapter hunt down deaths that teach nothing: Noita tracking instant kills ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 25:53](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1553)), Ultimate ADOM's traps that wound instead of kill ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 29:28](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1768)), Liotta's undo ([Colin Liotta 2018, 13:39](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=819)), Chogue's rooms that stay lit ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 17:26](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=1046)), bcrawl's fairness fixes ([bhauth 2020, 22:00](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=1320)) and Larsen's paid way out of an impossible puzzle ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 14:48](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=888)). Mike Cook instead accepts that a generator may produce unfair runs and designs scoring so that winning every run is not expected ([Mike Cook 2023, 21:06](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1266)), and Nic Tringali made sharp punishment part of The Banished Vault's identity ([Nic Tringali 2023, 7:17](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=437)), though the same team later started players on its easiest difficulty, and says it found the game hard to play itself ([Nic Tringali 2023, 28:32](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1712)). Moria shows the cost of tuning only for a hardcore few ([Santiago Zapata 2022, 8:59](https://youtu.be/y6WCq0jYbHo?t=539)). The choice depends on whether your audience shares the streak-and-score mindset Cook describes, and whether your theme can carry the harshness.

**Should runs make the player stronger?** Shawn Main argues players want their time rewarded ([Shawn Main 2021, 22:07](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1327)), and Jim Shepard that meta power softens permadeath and keeps players from quitting ([Jim Shepard 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=564)). Noita relies on knowledge alone ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 28:41](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1721)), and Tim Keenan, Andrew Aversa and John Harris warn of grind, of dying to build a character, and of the Wii Shiren's kept levels ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:42:37](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31357); [Andrew Aversa 2020, 26:31](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1591); [John Harris 2024, 19:48](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=1188)); even Shepard shows how meta power distorts both the early and late game ([Jim Shepard 2017, 12:24](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=744)). The middle paths in this chapter (faster early game, soft unlocks, capped carry-over, story and presence) suggest the question is less whether to carry anything over than which loop the reward lives in. It depends on whether your systems produce enough novelty that knowledge alone keeps runs fresh.

**Should permadeath be the default?** Aversa argues that if the experience you want to deliver is the late game, and you cannot make a varied early game without a heavy opening story, permadeath perhaps should not be the default ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 24:30](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1470)). Against that stand the reasons permadeath exists: the tension David Brevik fought to keep in Diablo ([David Brevik 2023, 6:58](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=418)), Todd Furmanski's precarious power narrative ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 4:47](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=287)), and Glenn Wichman's point that irreversibility is what gives decisions meaning ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 28:32](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1712)). The choice depends on where your content is: at the start of every run, or at the end of a long one.

**Smooth the swings, or keep them?** Shawn Main warns that games which smooth out uncertainty become flat micro-optimisation ([Shawn Main 2017, 19:57](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1197)), and Dylan Gedig accepts reduced agency in Peglin for memorable moments ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 25:03](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1503)); Evan Debenham and Sébastien Benard smooth deliberately ([Evan Debenham 2022, 1:39](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=99); [Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 28:59](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1739)). The audience test from John Harris's talk, whether players can build intuition for the randomness, is the best tie-breaker the talks offer ([John Harris 2016, 29:20](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1760)). Two speakers add a warning that cuts across the choice: pity timers can be addictive for people with gambling problems ([Ben Berman 2017, 33:30](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=2010)), and hidden fixed cycles can verge on dark patterns ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 28:40](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1720)).

**Hunger: clock or cruelty?** Tyriq Plummer removed starvation because it punished caution and pacifism ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 21:50](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1310)), and Thomas Biskup made hunger weaken but never kill ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:56](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1076)); Aversa's Tangledeep collapsed into kiting without a clock ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 12:44](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=764)). What decides it is whether anything else in your game makes waiting costly. Nicholas Feinberg's warning that strong clocks in a large game punish auto-explore ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 21:16](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=1276)) has no counter-position among the talks cited here: none describes a strong clock that coexists with travel automation.

**Can dominant strategies be removed?** Pandamander, Casey Yano, the Against the Storm team and Tringali all push to eliminate them ([Pandamander 2024, 15:21](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=921); [Casey Yano 2022, 28:45](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=1725); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 10:02](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=602); [Nic Tringali 2023, 19:17](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1157)). Tyler Coleman thinks about 20% of content will always dominate and prefers to keep that meta shifting ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 25:38](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1538)); Hades' bumpers bound build width without claiming to solve the problem ([Alice Lai 2021, 28:20](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1700)). The difference is ambition and budget: removing dominance needs content density, while managing it needs ongoing updates.

**A strict difficulty curve or a loose one?** Cat Burglar orders its question brackets so difficulty rises predictably ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 23:57](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1437)); Tim Keenan let a hard system arrive second in Duskers and got better stories, at the price of occasionally upsetting players ([Tim Keenan 2017, 13:49](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=829)). The choice is between a curve the player can trust and one that sometimes betrays them for drama.

**Nerf or buff?** Backpack Hero's data-driven nerfs drew criticism when the analytics behind them were public ([Jasper Cole 2023, 21:41](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1301)), while Dan DiIorio prefers buffing weak content, as Dota does, and found that tiny buffs turned losses into wins without alienating challenge-seekers ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 25:18](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=1518); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 15:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=910)). In a single-player game an overbuffed combo is a story, not an unfair edge; how far that holds with leaderboards or daily challenges is not discussed.

**Open questions.** In Q&A with Harry Solomons, the host asked whether runs could accrue burdens rather than upgrades; Solomons warned that a death which simply makes you worse breeds frustration ([Harry Solomons 2024, 26:17](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1577)). Leonard Richardson suggests grind could be subverted rather than removed ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 14:06](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=846)); none of the talks cited here reports trying it. Jeff Lait leaves open whether games should warn before a resource "wall" suddenly runs out ([Jeff Lait 2025, 11:48](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=708)).

## Checklist

1. What decisions in your game exist only because they cannot be undone, and is that list long enough to justify permadeath?
2. For each way the player can die, was there a readable warning, counterplay at the time, and a lesson the player can name?
3. How many seconds pass between death and the next real decision?
4. Is your variety concentrated at the start of the run, where permadeath guarantees it will be seen, and can a player pressing random keys survive the first stretch?
5. What is your target run length, and do you check major changes against it?
6. What does your default mode say about how the game should be played, and if you offer softer modes, have you designed hazards and the endgame for them?
7. What does a death leave behind (world state, a story, an item, power), and does it change what the next run is about or only how hard it is?
8. Which loop does each kind of progress live in, and does any meta power make the early game a walkover or the late game a grind wall?
9. For each random element, is it setup or result, and could a player who has died to it fifty times play better against it on the fifty-first?
10. Where do miss streaks, loot droughts or economy failures appear, and which smoothing tool fits each one?
11. Are the gambles you offer visible, voluntary and recoverable?
12. What would a player with infinite patience do with each system, and do your players blame deaths on skipped grind?
13. If you have a clock, what degenerate strategy does it stop, does it punish caution or automation, and does it leave quiet moments untimed?
14. Is there any option so strong that every run takes it?
15. Are your difficulty options granular, clearly labelled and respectful, and do harder tiers give a reason to play them?
